en: Abhinavagupta: Mālinīślokavārttika, First Section (Prathamaḥ Kāṇḍaḥ)

The Mother is the great new creation, whose basis is the stainless arts, and whose body is full; the Father is he whose splendor is hidden within the five faces. [I bow] to that which consists of the emission of the state vibrating from the union of those two.
May my heart, the family of unsurpassed nectar, radiate forth! // 1.1 //
May that Guru be victorious, by whose radiant rays of awakening our lotus-hearts have blossomed on all sides.
He who bestowed upon me floods of meaning— resplendent with the six touches, the three-and-a-half truths, and the five streams— and dedicated to the vow of crushing poverty.
May Śambhunātha— purified by the illustrious Sumati, compassionate toward his devoted followers, and gratified by the flower of my speech— be gracious unto me.
I pay homage to the one named Śrī Cukhla, who is more venerable even than my gurus; refined by his teachings, I stand free from all grasping. (1.5)
May the illustrious Bhūtirāja, the great-minded one who is even weightier than that, and who possesses the courage to uplift the multitude of his devotees, be victorious! 1.6 //
Victorious are the compositions of the fragrance of consciousness, issued forth from the illustrious Utpala and the awakening of Śrī Somānanda, which spread in all directions. 1.7.
Victorious is the word of the venerable teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta, who teaches the recognition that severs the cycle of transmigratory existence through that very vision. 1.8.
By this [work], my intellect-bee, intoxicated solely by the singular wonder of tasting the innumerable new [flavors], has been satiated with the unsurpassed enjoyment.
Having attained oneness with that and abiding thus within her very self,
various riches of sound (nāda) indeed manifest for her.
Requested again and again by the gentle ears of my true disciples, I shall explain the meaning of the words wherever they occur in the venerable *Mālinīvijaya*. (1.11)

In this [work], because of the mutual relationship between the signified and the signifier through appropriateness and the avoidance of the opposite, the treatise and the commentary proceed as a cycle of movement and non-movement. 1.12.
I bow to those Abhinavaguptas, who shine day and night within the range of no one else, and who are like a mass of rays from the moon of Śiva.
Victorious are the rays of the moon of knowledge arising from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, capable of destroying the adversaries of the world's bliss.
Because its true nature is unconditioned and it partakes solely in the non-duality of existence,
that great primordial wisdom which arose previously possesses the majestic splendor of a mass of rays.

That [reality] is thus pervasive, devoid of the notions of rejection and acceptance belonging to one's own māyā, and differentiated solely by the variegated rays of the manifestation of its expansion. // 1.16 //
That heart of the Supreme Lord has the nature of supreme touch;
even there, the Great Lord is eternally united with his own power, which consists of his very self.
When, having encountered friction, one attains the supreme meditative absorption (*samāpatti*),
then his supreme face becomes the locus for the expansion of emission (*visarga*).
The seed which exists as all things, beautiful with the bliss of the world arising from unsurpassed expansion, remains inseparable from the future face.

That which consists of the heart, vibration, vision, the supreme essence, the nameless, the wave, and so forth, is considered this supreme Trika, which is primordial and characterized by the non-differentiation of all powers.

In this state, due to the falling away from the expansion, apprehension, contraction, and cessation of objective existence, there remains only the triad of will, action, and perception, which consists solely of absorption in one's own bliss. (1.21)
And so the Gurus have described it thus in the *Śaivadarśana*: "When he remains absorbed in that experience which consists solely of the bliss of consciousness... (1.22).
To that extent is his will, to that extent is his knowledge, and to that extent is his action;
for he exists in the state of equilibrium among the three extremely subtle powers.
"Then, being of the nature of consciousness, he would become one with the supreme bliss;
for indeed, in such a state as this, which has become the self of the universe, there is an absence of contraction. (1.24)
"How can the excellence of the scriptures and so forth have their root in conceptual construction?
It is said: "All this cognition consists of the radiance of pure consciousness. (1.25)
Because it is conjoined with the nature of luminosity, it consists essentially of the dense awareness of consciousness (*cid-āmarśa*).
In that state, this very light which shines forth has awareness as its inherent nature. (1.26)
Why is that very flood of scripture not sufficient; what is the use of other displays of logic?
Pierced by the goddess of speech herself, it would be nothing more than that.
But it is not variegated by a collection of colors belonging to worldly illusion;
as it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*: "The manifestation [of objects] occurs while they reside within the Self. (1.28)
Indeed, reflective awareness proceeds without being separate from that [light]; otherwise, they know the nature of manifestation to be mere appearance devoid of reflection. (1.29)
Furthermore, illumination—even when colored by an object—is equal to gems and the like; moreover, whatever reflective awareness there may be, it is the domain of the wonder of consciousness. (1.30)

At that time, this [consciousness] becomes clearly manifest as objects such as pleasure and pain, by virtue of its union with the surging forth of the support for the internal reflective awareness of those [objects]. (1.31)
Subsequently, it becomes clearly manifest; and thus the Guru has said that pleasure and so forth are established as proven by one's own self-awareness. (1.32)

For at the time of its determination, that [object] is not experienced by self-awareness; therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that [self-awareness exists], because self-awareness is the means of proof. // 1.33 //
In the same way, here too, one should subsequently contemplate that ground consisting of the non-duality of all things, which exists on the path of the unfolding of knowledge and the rest. (1.34)
To that extent, by virtue of the clarity of those portions of noble reflection appropriate to it, that very prior emission attains the status of scripture (śāstra). // 1.35 //
But this alone would be appropriate, for even in the case of the supreme goal of the scripture, which is beyond all substrates, some trace of right conduct is still perceived. (1.36)
He is indeed possessed of the powers of primordial consciousness and the rest, which are the very locus of manifestation;
through that coloring, he is augmented by various diversities.
Just as the manifestation of a face occurs in water, a mirror, a gem, or a sword, there exists a state characterized by flickering, existence, circularity, subtlety, length, and so forth. (1.38)
Thus, in this supreme form, the riches of knowledge have arisen, beautiful as the triad of selves whose seed-nature resides in the uninterrupted heart. (1.39)

But when Bhairava, empowered by his own energy (śakti), desires to emit the flood of objective states (bhāvaugha) consisting of various internal waves whose forms emerge from him, [then the world arises]. (1.40)
Then those very perfections of consciousness, as it were, took refuge in the slight restraint of ritual practice born of that limiting adjunct. (1.41)
Nevertheless, even as the entire world has come to possess the nature of the flood of its waves, it remains beautiful with the bliss of the universe within the Bhairava of awakening.
When the powerful one is satisfied merely by the fullness of his own being, and the state of being a possessor of power has been eclipsed by his own perfect power alone; 1.43.
In that very same way, a stream of consciousness consisting of reflective awareness unfolds, within which a certain delight arises through the instruction on enjoyment. (1.44)
For the fortunate ones, even the multitude of enjoyments—when cultivated through the confidence arising from their consciousness, conduct, and practice—leads to the state of supreme bliss. (1.45)

It is said therein that the Lord’s fondness for sacrifice, which is filled with the intensity of the agitation of His own powers and so forth, arises specifically from the midst of the Mothers. (1.46)
Through the surging power of sovereignty, having attained the designation of the state of a Lord (īśvara), this deity—whose greatness is primordial wisdom—has arisen and been fully manifested. 1.47.

In this case as well, because the conjunction and disjunction of infinite constituent parts are maintained through the continuity of their prior distinct states, they are held to be innumerable. (1.48)

It is solely by virtue of those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that various manifestations of the power of scriptures, rituals, and knowledge—though devoid of the terms "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) and "cognition" (*jñāna*)—are extended. (1.49)
But this primary manifestation is analyzed as having a fivefold nature; and so it will be stated later: "The reality, though undivided, is fivefold. (1.50)

"Because [the Lord] possesses activity and sovereignty, because He is the impeller dependent upon that [activity], because His will has ceased, and because He is established in His own nature"—by such collections of statements as these. (1.51)
"Now, in such an extensive composition, do distinctions created by space, time, and artistic form not exist at all?
Indeed, we say: 'Certainly, Om! (1.52)
For here not even the mere name of the principle of time (kālatattva) is discerned; nor does the power of Mahākālī, who is pervasive throughout the future, manifest here. (1.53)
In that case, since it is non-different and self-sufficient, what indeed is the point of adopting such a verbal formulation as "then later" or "and again from another"? (1.54)

To this we reply: it is indeed true that, in reality, even when the manifestation of the principles has unfolded within its own clear nature, and even when time has opened its eyes within its own self; (1.55)
For consciousness, these conceptual constructions of "prior" and "posterior" do not exist at all, since time becomes a differentiator only by way of being a qualification. (1.56)
And that is declared to be a qualifier which, by way of being co-ordinate (samaśīrṣikayā), attains the state of being cognized as distinct, just as [one says] "the blue lotus. (1.57)
Furthermore, the state of being an object of knowledge for consciousness can never be logically established;
for being an object of knowledge means being manifest, and that [manifestation] occurs only through the grace of the light of consciousness itself. (1.58)

If that illumination were itself an awareness, it would require another awareness for its own existence; since there would be no rule governing such illumination, an infinite regress would certainly ensue. (1.59)
For this very reason, those who are utterly deluded—who would claim that awakening is non-manifesting while consisting of the manifestation of objects—are indeed deceived by their own words. (1.60)
Therefore, time is not capable of differentiating consciousness, nor is this time able to act as a differentiator of the object of knowledge. (1.61)
For the universe is non-different from consciousness; if it were otherwise, it would not manifest.
A diverse object shines forth when permeated by light. (1.62)
In this way, the universal illumination would be eternal for everyone; when that which is called consciousness exists as light, it attains the state of being illuminated. (1.63)
If an entity were non-luminous yet were perceived as having the nature of luminosity, then the only refuge for the claim that "this entity is indeed non-luminous" would be darkness itself. (1.64)
If that which is non-luminous by nature were made luminous, then that entity would surely be destroyed, because it has lost its own non-luminosity. (1.65)
Even the Creator is not capable of making that which is not of such a nature manifest;
for indeed, this state of "this-ness" appears only when there is manifestation.
Let this be so; however, let that which is thus unmanifest become manifest, provided that the non-manifestation of the entity has itself been made manifest. (1.67)

If it were the case that an entity is not manifested in this way, then that would be the actual state of things; therefore, there is no need for a separate manifestation, and Śiva is likewise [self-luminous]. (1.68)
Therefore, that which is sung of as the Supreme Śiva is indeed Light itself;
its greatness is inconceivable, and it is whirled about by the unrestrained power of its own absolute freedom.
In that same way, the state of the Immutable shines forth through those various natures; here, no one at all suspects the existence of an omniscient being anywhere. (1.70)
I, Caitra, know the jar, not the cloth; but he knows it.
This cloth does not know it.
Thus, I know: "the jar and the cloth. (1.71)
"I shall know it, or perhaps not;
previously I did not know it at all, nor anywhere; I know it gradually, simultaneously, by both means, or devoid of both. (1.72)
I know all, yet I know nothing at all. I am not any entity whatsoever, nor indeed am I; for I am both all and everything, at all times. // 1.73 //
"I alone am everything; what else could all this be?"—thus does this one Light alone manifest itself. (1.74)
If this [subject] were indeed one, then how could there be another manifestation? Oh, how can this fool be instructed! (1.75)
A single light manifests in variegated form through its own sovereignty; yet in reality, it is neither variegated—due to the refutation of duality—nor non-variegated. (1.76)
If the manifestation of a cloth were possible within the manifestation of a jar, that would not be the manifestation of the jar alone; for it would then be a dual manifestation. (1.77)
Let that indeed be so;
however, this which you have urged—that "its manifestation as the nature of a jar must not occur"—is not the case. Thus it remains [as stated]. (1.78)
And that is illogical; for since light is consciousness, if its characteristic is simply its own unfolding, then what is the point of this vain display of verbal proliferation? (1.79)
Limited luminosity is indeed the defining characteristic of the insentient; for consciousness, which is distinct from the insentient, is not so measured. (1.80)
Therefore, since the existence of the sun is established, what fool indeed could say:
"How is it that he [the Lord] has filled the entire earth with the splendor of his own rays? (1.81)
Therefore, once this Light is established, all conceptualizations regarding that Light are merely the observance of the conduct of a wife shared by all. (1.82)
And if illumination were unestablished, who would I be, what would you be, and what even would darkness be?
Would there be nothing at all, or how could one even remain silent? (1.83)
Therefore, for even those entities that have attained the state of Bhairava through identity with the Light,
this time is unable to do anything at all.
Well then, let the sequence of words beginning with "how so" (kathaṃkāram) be heard; although this has already been stated, it is being said again by breaking it down further. 1.85.
That which is luminosity appears as this very thing in such and such ways;
it does not appear as anything else at all, yet it shines forth in its own right.
He alone is supremely noble, the illuminator of all, and independent; thus, His power of will is designated as "sovereignty" (svātantrya). (1.87)
And that [consciousness], resting within itself due to the absence of anything other than itself, is said to be this very rest within its own self, which is the bliss of the Lord. (1.88)
The very majesty of His sovereignty, which exists inseparable from His own nature, may manifest the delusions of objective phenomena within His own self-luminous abode. (1.89)

And it is stated in the scriptures that manifestation is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), by which the differentiation of the various categories of reality (*tattva*) and so forth is brought about. (1.90)
And how indeed could that manifestation which resides within it be conceived if it were not manifest? I am remembered as its power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). (1.91)
That which is the form of this God consisting solely of his own self is called "unmeṣa" (the unfolding); from that, the all-pervasive Lord [manifests] the five powers.
Whether as the three powers or as a single power, whether as the God alone or as the Goddess who is indeed Power—this is what is described in the Sāraśāstra. (1.93)

And it will be stated by the Great Lord [Maheśvara] later than this point, beginning with the words "The element of the world has been described," that this very one, though singular, attains manifoldness. (1.94)
And this very [reality], firmly established in its own self through rest in intense bliss, is expressed by Bhairava and others in their congenial compositions of words. (1.95)
Whether it be near or far away, even if there were not actually any collection of sounds belonging to him, or even if there were something else belonging to the Lord, O Master.
And so, this Lord indeed manifests in such and such ways;
therefore, this entire sequence of conceptual construction follows accordingly.
Nor is that [world] merely a mental construction; even if it were so, what harm would there be? Let the Lord will it as such, or let him construct it as such. (1.98)
And thus this Lord, whose nature is light and who transcends the thirty-sevenfold [principles], manifests time by bringing about the appearance of manifold variety. (1.99)
This very manifestation of diversity is declared to be the power of time; therefore, in accordance with this manifesting power of time, [the following occurs]. (1.100)
The obscuration beginning with "from our [view]" and so forth proceeds;
yet it is not the case that this does not exist there at all. For how could that which does not exist there [be produced]? (1.101)
Otherwise, that which is called "alterity" would remain subject to manifestation;
surely, this being so, it applies to other networks of principles (*tattva*) as well, in their states of purity or impurity. (1.102)
Whether it be in the pure or impure state, or in the mandala of the principles (tattva) beginning with Vidyā, there will be no distinction because of the presence of the true being of Śuddhabhairava.
Alas, we dance about with effort; indeed, that which revolves of its own accord within the heart of your long-lived self must certainly be explained by us.
Indeed, the distinction between pure and impure does not exist in discussions concerning the ultimate truth; rather, it remains fixed only in the minds of the deluded, created by them alone.
Now, if the distinction called "purity and impurity" is not real, then this very scripture that you wish to explain would be contradicting itself. (1.106)
"For the impurity of the principles is purified by initiation," and so forth; since the state [described] here is predominantly characterized by manifold distinctions. (1.107)
It is said: in that non-dual reality, duality does not exist at all in any way;
for it has been stated that even in the all-pervading Lord, who is devoid of division, there is the appearance of division. (1.108)
Indeed, that very [nature] is called "bondage" in saṃsāra by such terms as *māyā* and *avidyā*; those who are established therein are considered to be transmigrating beings. (1.109)
Because they follow after such contemplation, there arises for them the determination of what is pure, impure, and so forth;
moreover, this scripture is the perfect teacher of the yoga of the Blessed One.
They declare that the yoga of the Blessed One is non-dual and free from the pairs of opposites;
its instruction would be thus, if it were characterized by differentiation to any degree whatsoever.
That which is conceived is analyzed again and again,
even as one enters and settles within the all-pervasive Lord Bhairava in non-duality.
There is no state resulting from repeated practice, for those two [dualities] have difference alone as their lifeblood;
therefore, in order to dispel all possible doubts regarding duality: (1.113)
Since every effort of both teachers and students unfolds from this, all [this work] is elaborated here by repeatedly raising and resolving doubts regarding duality. (1.114)
Therefore, one should investigate as far as possible and never remain indifferent;
for if duality has not been scrutinized, then [reality] would be merely a single entity. (1.115)
That Brahman is consciousness alone; therefore, what is the use of determining the enumeration of principles? Why is it described that there are thirty-five principles? // 1.116 //
Therefore, having grasped the dualistic state of existence as it appears until the very end of its course, one should achieve freedom from doubt by means of its subsequent rejection. (1.117)
And this very instruction, which pierces right through consciousness, is the tearing asunder of the "vajra-wings" (the subtle body) according to their respective possibilities. (1.118)
For thus it is said by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa in his *Śrīstotra*:
"Salutations to You, who, having brought forth the delusion of those bewildered by worldly existence, shatter that very delusion. (1.119)
And having chosen the bliss of knowledge, which is free from dualities, O Lord, they reveal it;
by the term "free from dualities," the non-dual state is made manifest. (1.120)
And the word "ca" (and) here is strikingly significant, as it implies that errors are also being pointed out;
furthermore, it will be demonstrated later that in this system, non-duality alone is the truth.

It will be stated that the purification of the paths and so forth are untenable in a state of duality; yet, is it not the case that these cannot exist without non-duality? Indeed, why should they not exist even without duality? (1.122)

It is true; however, even difference is not untenable within the non-dual reality, for this is indeed that supreme non-duality in which there is neither the abandonment nor the grasping of difference.

But since all phenomena are established in their own respective natures within the context of difference, I think this word "non-difference" (abheda) actually differentiates them from the perspective of aesthetic flavor (rasa). 1.124.
Therefore, enough; let the subject at hand be examined:
the Supreme Lord indeed manifests the conceptualization of duality in whatever manner it may be.
But surely time also expands in that same way? 1.125.
Nevertheless, it never undergoes division in the ultimate sense,
for it is always of the nature of consciousness and exists simultaneously.
Now, in this consciousness whose essence is the reflective awareness of a single, compact state, whatever I— who am manifold— do or know, others such as Maitra and Caitra do not [experience that].
Or else, how could they not know? // 1.127 //
Oh, how exceedingly dense is this knot of illusion for you!
For we declare here that there is not even a single thing called "self" or "other";
rather, the notion "I know this" is merely the manifestation of a particular form, such as a jar or a body.
It has been stated that various diverse forms shine within the supreme light. // 1.128 //

Therefore, in the cognition "I know the jar," there is indeed no difference [between the self and the object]; yet, is it not the case that the appearance of difference exists in the form "this jar appears to me"?
This is not the case; for him, this [world] is likewise Śiva.
For this very reason, Dvaipāyana and other leaders have declared that attachment (*mamakāra*) itself is death within their own scriptural domains, because it brings about refutation. (1.130)
Thus, in this manner, cognitions—even within the supreme reality—manifest as "that time" and so forth, arising from the coloring produced by the limiting adjunct of the measurement of time. (1.131)
In that regard, because it is of a single complete nature, everything exists everywhere; otherwise, since fragmentation would be impossible, completeness itself could not be complete. (1.132)
Then, in its fullness within the abode of Sarvasahabhairava, this fivefold meaning of the scripture is Śāmbhava; [it concerns] the state of the power and the individual soul.

Having suppressed the supreme Goddess within himself and having caused her to overflow within his own self, he thus exists as one desiring to emit, [projecting] entities from the state of being the emitter.
Previously, he had attained a state of dense, surging bliss; now, in the position of the Creator, he even partakes in the immersion of emission.

While becoming emptied by means of the full consciousness that is a mass of bliss, it is nevertheless filled with the intense immersion into the emission (*visarga*) which is a portion of the power of bliss.
Existing as full with the flood of its own power, it will become empty of power; thus, it consists of the manifold experience of these three natures.
Then he would clearly be a god among gods in the state of the creator;
for surely, what connection could there be between the present part and the past and future?
What indeed have you understood? Even in your own system, some maintain that the past and the future are distinguished by means of the present limit. (1.139)
And how could that which has not come to rest anywhere be divided?
Furthermore, for you, how could there be the status of a limit for the present?
Or how could those two possess a limit even with respect to that [universe]?
Why does the universe not likewise arise such that the universe itself is its own limit? (1.141)
Therefore, since the past and the future are indeed rooted in the consciousness known as the present, one should find rest in that alone. 1.142.
And if one were to remain for a moment right here, with one's own state completely restrained, without expanding the entire circle of rays of conceptual construction; (1.143)
It attains a singular savoring of the wonder of its own expanding nectar, which carries forth a flood of the ambrosia of supreme bliss.
For instance, when the moon is completely filled by the flood of the sun's rays, it does not emit its own rays as long as [the sun] continues to shine upon it. (1.145)
For that long, well-settled in a moment of rest within the expanse of one's own mandala, one is said to be a vessel for the satiation of the portions of all the deities residing within. (1.146)
Thus, while the moonlight of one’s own awakening shines within the heart, it is filled with a mass of rays from the sun that illuminates all phenomena.
Since he has found rest within that which is beautiful with the essence of the nectar of the noble consciousness abiding inside, the internal flood of his own immortality is not vomited out.
Then, right there within that very space, he whirled about and surged upward,
consisting of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃvid*) which satisfies the circle of deities residing within his own heart.

The sequence of one's own faculties arises as long as they are being aroused; however, when the mass of rays is ceased through the yoga of the non-existence of phenomenal manifestation, [the faculties cease]. (1.150)
The past does not exist apart from the present, nor will the future; as long as there is no distinction between those two, how can there be such a thing as "presentness"? (1.151)
For she attains a state of differentiation through her past and future natures;
therefore, having rested for a mere moment within this limit of consciousness, [she proceeds].
The yogi intent on seizing time becomes a sky-walker in an instant; for it has been said: "That which is the appearance of existence is time, and that consists of calculation. (1.153)
The expansion of the rays of one's own consciousness is neither existence nor non-existence; it is nothing other than that.
Therefore, by blocking the gateway of one's own rays, the entire circle of the paths is obstructed.
"One who takes delight solely in devouring time becomes a sky-farer (khecara) by himself";
this was stated by the Supreme Lord in the Tantra named Śrīḍāmara.
Having restrained one's own wheel of rays and having drunk the unsurpassed nectar,
one shall become happy while abiding in the present, which is not delimited by the two extremes of time.
In this [reality] which is devoid of contraction, there is no such thing as obstruction;
because that [obstruction] is absent, there is no expansion either. Likewise, how could there be "swallowing" or "satiety" here? 1.157.
However, according to the principle already stated, the blocking, expanding, swallowing, and so forth appear;
yet, apart from such appearance, there is no other entity whatsoever anywhere in the universe. (1.158)
Thus, enough with this extensive talk in the assembly of the circle of sky-farers;
for what connection is there between Abhinavagupta and this sequence of direct experience? (1.159)
We shall now speak of the subject at hand: those manifold cognitions emitted by the Goddess, which extend as far as that ever-ascending stream which is devoid of differentiation.
From that, the Saurabhargaśikhā and other scriptures were composed; and it was stated in the Bhargaśikhā by the Supreme Lord: 1.161 //

O Dear One, this supreme knowledge arises from the upward flow (ūrdhvasrotas); it is expressed by the "Supreme Path" (paramadhvani), which denotes the nature of consciousness that ascends higher and higher.
He taught a distinction from the Siddhānta that emerged from the mouth of Īśāna;
here too, they are variegated by being interspersed with portions of the previous divisions.
As long as this primary lineage of sixfold scriptures exists here, those various scholars expand their respective divergent interpretations of the treatises. 1.164.
Those Trika scriptures which constitute the first half of this [tradition] have been sufficiently expounded by the teachers under the designation of "Half-of-Six" (Ṣaḍardha).
But this sequence of words is not [intended] solely because of its hidden mystery;
for otherwise, why would there not also be such expressions as "twelve half-halves" and so forth? (1.166)
In this regard, the triad of powers is considered to be in a state of complete perfection; they exist without mutual obstruction, full and consisting of the nature of perfect consciousness. (1.167)
Beyond that, however, when a certain [set] possesses the state of being multiplied and another possesses the state of being a multiplier, they are designated as a "pair" (yāmala). (1.168)

Thereafter, when the flood of objects has been emitted, due to the connection with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of their diversity, the five powers of one's own self—which are characterized by both differentiation and non-differentiation—[arise]. (1.169)

By virtue of its own inherent fitness, [consciousness] arises from the five auspicious limbs of Brahman— consisting of consciousness, vibration, will, knowledge, and action— as the awakening of the aspect of being that manifests.
Form, having attained the nature of the scripture, unfolds in exactly five ways; for thus, first, there is the unfolding of the flood of entities abiding within the infinite interior. (1.171)
To whatever extent the Blessed One acts, to that same extent he abides in the face of Īśa; this occurs during the unfolding of the internal, undivided power of action (kriyā-śakti). 1.172.
When that [power] unfolds in due order, this entire expansion of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) extends clearly; this manifest expansion will attain the state of Māyā.
For it will be stated that within the very nature of the principle of Māyā resides Śivā-Īśānī, who brings about the manifestation of the universe—pure, impure-pure, and entirely impure. (1.174)
For Śambhu, whose body consists of the five mantras, there is indeed an association with the impure that is to be emanated; for everything is established within the prior limit [of time]. (1.175)
For instance, when someone desires to go somewhere from their own home, whatever distance is to be traversed in the first moment, and whatever lies within that interval— ||| 1.176 ||

Even at the falling away of a *tuṭi*, there is the attainment of omniscience and omnipotence for those whose nature is steady in the excellence of the specific portion [of reality] precisely because of that. (1.177)
For in this way, the cognition—comparable to the touch of the edge of a blade of genuine steel—extracts the specific features at the very same moment it flashes forth. (1.178)

One whose wisdom is clarified by the reality of the jewels gathers those various specific qualities of even the most abundant gems, as they are revealed at that very moment like flashes of lightning. (1.179)
One who is absorbed in that [art] perceives the variety within a single expanse of the lute, which is joined with the lightness of touch and the accumulation of many tones. (1.180)

One whose faculty of hearing has come to rest upon the crest of a continuous stream of intense practice indeed perceives even the internal excess or deficiency of the *śruti*s within the components of those notes. (1.181)
Let this [point] rest; it is established without effort in this doctrine of non-duality, wherein even though difference appears, there is in reality non-duality. (1.182)

As long as this [distinction] remains clearly established in a treatise whose very life is duality, so indeed has it been stated by Patañjali in the chapter named "Vibhūti" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 3.24): [1.183]

Or else, "everything is manifested through intuitive insight" (*prātibha*); and here, even for me, within that first flash of intuitive insight which is the undivided nature of consciousness, [all things are manifest]. (1.184)
Abiding as the self of all radiance, the source from which the fruit of all accomplishments arises, he has forcibly assumed the desire to create within this world that is yet to be fashioned. (1.185)
Though impure and though capable of the various diversities of its own form, it is nevertheless beautiful as a part through its differentiation, by way of its universal aspect.
This very state, consisting of both difference and non-difference, remains fully manifest;
for this reason, it abides in that which is called Sādākhya, whose nature is the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti). (1.187)
Due to the turbidity of even a slight trace of impurity, there exists a state of being both higher and lower;
therefore, even from this [state] which has been tasted by the Lord, one partakes of the higher plane.
Out of eagerness to manifest his illusory power, and likewise due to the persistence of its latent impressions,
he engaged in various consultations consisting of the undertaking of many activities.
And that which has appeared from the great continuity of wisdom bestows auspiciousness; for therein it is another state, with the other state obscured. (1.190)

But one should not attain established status [in this system] like those who follow impure higher paths; for that reason, those who are devoted to other teachings such as Vaiṣṇava or Buddhist doctrines [are excluded]. (1.191)

Those who are consecrated by the Śaiva [tradition] are not liberated in the same way as those who do not correctly [follow their path] within the Atimārga, Krama, Kula, Trika, Srotas, Antara, and other [systems]. (1.192)
But for those men who have been properly initiated into the scripture of the Supreme Lord (Parameśāna), there is no difference whatsoever in their attainment of liberation. (1.193)
Nor is there any other means to liberation besides this, except perhaps in certain cases through the effortless attainment of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). (1.194)

"Supreme perfection is attained very quickly according to our systems; whereas elsewhere, it is achieved only after a long time through the sequence of the stages of yoga and the series of the principles. (1.195)
And by means of various such sets of ritual acts, the supreme fruit is obtained;
for this very reason, here in this world, there exists even the Kaulika vision for those who possess the vision of reabsorption.

As it was stated in the *Kālapāda* and other texts, "one should initiate even outcastes (*śvapaca*)," there are five [stages] beginning with the unfolding of consciousness (*cid-unmeṣa*), which were previously [described] as being non-different from the beginning. (1.197)

These very [energies] were proclaimed in their collective totality within Bhairava, the Supreme Lord of Consciousness; yet they are manifested as differentiated by the limiting adjuncts of objective states. (1.198)
Even those who previously experienced non-difference are quite capable of nourishing only the aspect of difference;
for instance, the consumption of rice that serves to nourish the body [is distinct from the act of eating]. (1.199)
Indeed, through the falling away of accumulated phlegm, that [wind] causes the decay of the body;
for even though the Lord is the self of the universe, he does not fall from his own nature.

How could there be the occurrence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) that are subject to modification within Bhairava himself, who is the source of all states of being? For it is only among those things subject to modification that the operation of such adjuncts is possible; therefore, any perceived diversity arises solely through the influence of those adjuncts.
Thus, it is indeed an extreme rashness to think that changeable states ought not to ascend into the realm of our minds, as if they were non-existent. 1.202.
That very God, the soul of the universe, shines forth in such a form; though he is without limiting adjuncts and undivided, there is an appearance of division due to limiting adjuncts. (1.203)
Surely, in this way, that would be unreal; for how could that very thing be real?
Since it appears in such a manner, what else could be established as real anywhere? 1.204.
Now, if this is so, is the cycle of existence in a dream real? Rather, it is indeed treated as unreal because it is barren of the desired performance of purposeful action. (1.205)
And this will be established in detail through reasoning further on; therefore, that power of unfolding which previously existed as non-dual... (1.206)
Having attained the state of Tatpuruṣa, which is the very nature of the unfolding of existence,
that which is non-different [from it] is ungraspable, and that which is the grasper is Īśvara.

Now, that which is established as the object to be grasped is distinct; the grasper of it is likewise distinct, and is therefore called "Puruṣa" (the Spirit) due to its connection with the commencement of creation. (1.208)
Because it is clearly recognized [as such], it is called the primary face;
for this very reason, it obstructs the persistence of the state of emission (visarga) here. (1.209)

Various collections of diseases, planetary afflictions, poisons, and the like are examined; [those who are] well-established, with their multitude of illnesses shattered by manifold methods, are brought to peace. // 1.210 //
In this state, all entities that function solely through differentiation attain complete clarity;
for that which constitutes the very nature of all entities is this primordial face. (1.211)
And because of the excellence of his qualities in every respect, Īśāna has an upward-facing aspect;
however, in that which is devoid of the reckoning of space and time, there is no conceptualization of spatial distinctions.
For he who is superior in qualities compared to another will become "higher" than him;
thus, when he desires things correctly through the manifestation of his will, [he attains them]. (1.213)
When they have ascended into that will, and that will itself is stainless, then, through the yoga of identity with that, these [beings] touch oneness with consciousness. (1.214)
However, at that time those entities remained with their desires obscured and concealed by the veil of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), whereas the Lord himself remained established in his own desire.
With his face turned toward consciousness that has receded, he does not abide in the full, supreme state; therefore, he appears as if in deep sleep. // 1.216 //
And because he is awakened, he is not asleep; for in the ultimate sense, there is no "closing" (nimīlana) of sleep for one whose consciousness is the bliss of Bhairava. (1.217)
For when that supreme light has indeed entered a state of closure due to dissolution, where could even the cognition of its closure appear? (1.218)
And no object remains unmanifested, like the view from a window in a house situated in the sky;
or rather, even that imagined form shines forth within the light of consciousness. (1.219)
Thus, though his eyes are not actually closed, he remains as if they were; for the power of lords who accomplish the impossible is indeed inconceivable.
"This is accomplished through happiness, but that is accomplished through suffering"—in this variety of appearances, he alone is our independent [agent]. (1.221)
That very sovereignty of his is the power called Niyati, by which the bound soul (paśu) is obstructed so that he never attains sovereignty at all. (1.222)
It is on account of that dependence that the Lord's performance of what is difficult to accomplish is proclaimed;
for indeed, nothing whatsoever is either easy or difficult to accomplish for the Soul of the Universe.
Why has this been examined by him again and again so many times? Alas, this would be useless for one such as you, whose nature is forgetfulness.
"But why direct such vehemence toward this single object?
For do the clouds of the rainy season pour forth their waters merely for the sake of producing a single sprout? (1.225)
And this is a vital point here, for that person who is to be instructed is pervaded by the ground of the heart, which has been drawn down by the flood of karma due to its extreme delicacy. (1.226)
By means of the sprouts and stalks of endless conceptual constructions arising from the seed of *māyā*, which are cultivated through speech born of the conceit of duality, // 1.227 //
As long as this great fire of knowledge has not been kindled again and again, so long will this duality of his sprout forth again and again. (1.228)
Once the tree of dualistic differentiation has been split apart by the floods of sharp analytical axes, kindled by the fire of true knowledge, it will never sprout again.
In this way, while the Lord occupies the state of deep sleep, even existing entities become as if non-existent, like a wood-apple fruit in a chasm. (1.230)
In this state, his own knowledge, being exactly such— filled with dispassion, indefinable, and without support— unfolded itself through differentiation.
Adorned with garlands of skulls, dwelling in the grounds of cremation grounds, they have turned their backs on us and range over the domains of the hosts of spirits.
Everything that is to be enjoyed is indeed limited by repulsiveness;
for who am I, the enjoyer? This body is merely skin and bone, and there is no essence in it.
It exists even in the slightest portion or fraction at some time. // 1.233 //
Practicing in this manner, they ascend to the highest perfection of dispassion at every moment and then, struck down by that, they fall into sleep.
Thinking "What is this?", the functions of the senses rush even toward suffering;
thinking "This is thus," they generally become dispassionate even toward pleasure. (1.235)
When there is freedom from thirst for the flood of objects seen or heard, the intellect attains mastery;
beyond that is the freedom from thirst for the *guṇas* resulting from the discernment of the *puruṣa*. (1.236)
Indeed, even though it is not the proper occasion, we shall ask something, provided you do not grow angry:
why [is there a distinction] at the limit where the jar, which is the occasion for the destruction of the occasion for destruction, is destroyed out of season? (1.237)
If this consciousness is thus pure by its very nature, why does it yearn with such intensity for enjoyments that are inherently impure? (1.238)
Indeed, where has your pride in possessing a nature free from forgetfulness gone now?
Enough with these reproaches against the intellect; even though this has already been said, it is stated once more.
For it has been explained that consciousness, by its very nature, is the ultimate reality of luminosity; it appears through its connection with the manifestation of the entire universe. (1.240)
And therefore, since the Goddess of Consciousness surges forth within Her own self amidst the entire circle of objective phenomena, how could any fragmentation possibly arise? (1.241)
Even when duality is manifested by the power of the Supreme Lord, it is analyzed that consciousness nevertheless runs toward [and permeates] all entities. (1.242)
Just as a clod of earth, a pool, a flame, a breath, a jar, and the state of space [respectively] possess the nature of the earth, water, great fire, wind, and infinite void; 1.243.
This consciousness, having emerged from itself in the form of cognition, indeed proceeds in succession and pursues only those objects that are of the same nature as the form of consciousness. (1.244)
And thus it was perceived by some supreme lord:
"Who is capable of setting in motion this water of a sunken pond? (1.245)
Furthermore, when that [stream] is complete, do the flows not indeed proceed in all directions? Is it not thus, by the power of its own necessity, that some [beings] alone [attain this]? (1.246)
In this way, that body of hers, whose essence is the principle of passion (rāga-tattva), runs about; and even therein, let that very appearance of passion be maintained as such. (1.247)
But let there be some form of passion within the conscious self (cidātman) consisting of the coloring by another;
if this is so, how indeed could that [passion] ever become dispassionate toward anything? (1.248)
Ah! This very discussion has come to bear upon the subject at hand, for when this consciousness itself exists in a state of contraction in every respect. (1.249)

Gradually, it becomes empty—like that which undergoes the great dissolution—with respect to the means of enjoyment, the objects of enjoyment, the body, the enjoyer, and likewise the act of enjoying. (1.250)
This state is born in the form of Rudra because it is destructive (sāṃhārikī),
and since Rudra is Sadyojāta and Puruṣa is of the nature of Īśvara.
The glorious Lord Sadāśiva is celebrated as Īśāna; Viṣṇu shall be Vāma, and Aghora shall be Brahmā. (1.252)
Because each one of these nourishes by virtue of containing all powers within itself, and because it is great and nourishes the universe, they are called "Brahmāṇīs. (1.253)
For this very reason, when the predominance of one of the other powers is intended to be expressed, each [of those powers] possesses a connection with the five causes beginning with Brahmā.
That very [state] is elaborated in various ways through different divisions in those respective scriptures;
therefore, in this Sadyojāta, the primary state of Raudra is established. (1.255)
And although she is of the nature of contraction, she will exist within the expansion of consciousness; because the portions of Brahmā and Viṣṇu are dissolved therein, she forcibly subordinates them.
The state beginning with "consisting of the non-existence of objects" and so forth has Rudra as its presiding deity;
this is the distinct object of knowledge, as described by the venerable Utpala. (1.257)

Although [the subject] has arisen within the subtle elements of differentiation, because it undergoes contraction therein, the enjoyer and the enjoyed here clearly become obscured from one another. (1.258)
This entire universe appears here instantly as if unborn;
therefore, the state of the "Sadyojāta" (the newly born) consists of the self-awareness of emptiness.
Then, as soon as that deity intends to enter within the state of emptiness, the entire universe, already established, surges forth spontaneously within his own awakening.

This power of knowledge of the Lord, which causes expansion, knows [all things]; thus, the state of absorption within the abode of expanding consciousness of those two has been established. // 1.261 //
The expansion of that consciousness, which is of the nature of emptiness, is indeed the universe itself.
For it is thus: [the mind] is filled with the intensity of resting in a dense, deep sleep. (1.262)
One recognizes those various portions of houses, shops, and so forth as being designated by the term "dream-state";
for this very reason, that is not a creation, but rather it is a state of persistence (sthiti) in that manner. (1.263)
For that which consists of mere cognition exists within the entities created previously; likewise, a dream arises as distinct from the form perceived while awake. (1.264)
However, since the manifold subdivisions of each state, such as waking and so forth,
will be determined later, it is therefore appropriate that they appear in the form of creation.
Therefore, the all-pervading Lord, pervading those states through his own awakening, causes them to relinquish that state of neutrality which belongs to him. (1.266)
This is the unfolding of the power of consciousness; for those entities that exist within that knowledge, their own radiance blossoming, they attain fullness.
Indeed, there would be a supreme contraction at the stage of the "newly born" (sadyojāta), insofar as no finality regarding their own true nature ever arises. (1.268)
Without the ascent of consciousness, how could the distinctions between existence and non-existence, the insentient and the sentient, or "blue" and "not blue," and so forth, be established? (1.269)
As the venerable Utpala said: "It is certain that there is no distinction in their own nature between the existent and the non-existent, nor between the insentient and the sentient. (1.270)
Therefore, emitting on all sides the beautiful bliss that animates consciousness, [he emits] the state of self and other projected by the radiance of the burden of awakening. (1.271)

Desiring to appropriate the universe by means of his singular body of consciousness, that God is called "Vāma" because he emits the power of his own awakening within the self of consciousness. (1.272)

Although this [Lord] bestows such forms upon entities through the intensification of his own power of consciousness, nevertheless, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), it remains as it is.
Desiring to appropriate their destruction, he ordains distinctions;
therefore, in the establishment of duality, this Supreme Lord is the "Left-hand" (Vāma). 1.274.
In this context, that kind of knowledge which flows from good fortune is extended; and "good fortune" is said to be the very acceptance of those [objects] as distinct. (1.275)

And that consciousness which, by its own power, surges forth from the sight of the various wonders of its own creative artistry—the diverse phenomena that constitute the instruments of experience—[is the true nature of the Self]. (1.276)
For it is she alone who, through her inherent passion (*svabhāvarāga*), colors the universe;
for only when manifested does she color the universe, and her manifestation occurs by virtue of her own essential nature.
That very state of surging forth, the arising of the fullness of the desire to accept, remains for a moment with undivided attention upon the entire essence of its radiance. (1.278)
What does he not attract, and what does this knower of yoga not cultivate?
For that very reason it is said in the treatise: "One who is not impassioned should cause [the mind] to be impassioned. (1.279)
One situated in desire, standing in the midst of desire, and encased within the goad of desire, should accomplish desires through desire; one should employ desire among desires. // 1.280 //

Desire is simply the wish to appropriate; through the application of concealing that [desire], the one possessed by desire accomplishes the universe, because this is the very essence of desire. (1.281)
For thus, having firmly established oneself in the supreme Self,
one immediately proceeds through the process of veiling the power of awakening that has surged forth from it.
The entire universe appears as a servant, subject to the goad of desire;
yet, through this very logic of spiritual realization, it does so upon its own arising.

The vital breath (prāṇa), pervading the body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka) and the universe, draws [them] forth, because it manifests the reality of the principle of desire (kāmatattva). // 1.284 //
Among the circles of the Siddhas, what is this that is to be hidden, or what has not been made manifest?
For the Lord, having issued forth from the bliss of the void, is of a nature that surges upward.
The omnipresent Lord proceeds by expanding His own powers only toward that which He desires to enter and from which He has previously withdrawn.
This reality exists having intensified all powers within its own self; therefore, the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, appears as if he were latent. (1.287)
But when they have arisen, these [powers]—expansion, will, knowledge, and action—shine forth;
therefore, although he appears as endowed with this tetrad, [he remains essentially one]. (1.288)
Nevertheless, how could there actually be a calculation of its powers, since it is precisely here that the art of uprooting the portions of the distinctions of existence occurs? (1.289)
Therefore, the conduct established therein has a sphere of activity that transcends the world;
yet, due to the manifold variety of infinite powers, even here [in this system] there are rites such as *uccāṭana* (exorcism) and so forth. (1.290)

Even those various activities, though primarily characterized by the play of withdrawal, remain present; thus, while the body of all entities remains within the sphere of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). // 1.291 //
Then, at the ultimate limit, the power of action itself respectfully withdraws those [powers],
just as the most subtle power called *unmeṣa* does at the supreme boundary.
Just as [consciousness] appears in a gross form due to the grossness of the objects to be created, so too does this power of action (kriyā-śakti), within which all entities are made to blink. (1.293)
Abiding in its own essential nature, some indefinable reality unfolds as if full;
indeed, there exists an action in which duality appears. (1.294)
Let it not be so; rather, every action first precludes difference.
For instance, those things such as wood, fire, and rice that exist on the level of differentiation—*kāṣṭhajvalanataṇḍulāḥ*—[are thus negated]. (1.295)
If those very things, when permeated by the process of cooking, respectfully abandon their distinction, then how could there be a unity of cooking for them if they possess distinct natures? (1.296)
Indeed, a distinct intrinsic nature for the constituent parts is not logically tenable; for there is no such thing as "cooking" that possesses a manifold nature. (1.297)
Flaming, moistening, burning, and so forth—these are designated by the term "maturation" (pāka); all these distinct actions are established as being directed toward a single result. (1.298)
It is called "cooking" (pāka); there is no other action whatsoever by this name.
How is it that many [actions] can have one desired result? (1.299)
How could those [images] be accomplished? From the very reason stated previously:
"Is it not clear that [the object appears] even through mental attention directed toward the eye, a lamp, or other objects? (1.300)
A single cognition is produced; it will likewise be thus in this case:
"This is he, whose body has been soiled by contact with mud."
One who desires to bathe runs toward the waters of a mirage in the desert;
for it is possible that a single entity exists despite its diverse appearances. (1.302)

In that case, the difference [between things] due to a difference in their causes is not ultimate; for otherwise, one would have to accept that it is a single entity while possessing a differentiated nature. (1.303)
If it is argued that "a difference in intrinsic nature leads to [a difference in action]," then this vow would be abandoned;
for in that case, let there be no single action, since wood and other such things are [distinct] causal factors (*kāraka*). (1.304)
Even if it were so that [the capacity] produces the fruit, there would be no harm to us; for we do not admit any action other than this very capacity from which [the result arises]. (1.305)
And that power, through the conceptualization of diverse fruits, is essentially the Being itself due to its non-differentiation;
and that power belongs to the All-pervasive One alone, who is the embodiment of the essence of the universe.

In ultimate reality, they are not divided by the distinction between the result and the agent; for although the all-pervasive [Self] is non-dual within its own nature, it appears as such through this manifestation of differentiation. (1.307)
That by which the Great Lord (Maheśvara) acts is called the power of action (kriyā-śakti); but how can that which animals (paśus) might perform be logically established? (1.308)

For since they subsist solely through differentiation, they would perform actions characterized by difference; enough with this [objection], for it is clear how animals could possibly act otherwise. (1.309)
That very argument is cut off by his own words, like the son of a barren woman;
for a potter can never, at any time or place, be the creator [of himself]. (1.310)
If that [pot] does not partake in non-difference from its maker, who is known as Maheśa, then surely is the pot also made by a potter? (1.311)
If the Lord is the creator of the universe, why does he not also exercise agency over a cloth?
If that were so, why would the potter not also produce a cloth? (1.312)
But if this were so, since there would be no other agent at all, for whom could the causality of good and bad actions exist in order to produce their own respective fruits? (1.313)
"It is just so, venerable sir; for indeed, for those who understand in this way, there is no fruit whatsoever arising from the auspicious or the inauspicious anywhere. (1.314)
Thus, those who do not know this eat [the fruit] while remaining unwise; that very thing, known by the name "action," is impurity rooted in ignorance. (1.315)
Having accepted exactly this [position], some indeed maintain that there is only pure consciousness, which is a non-agent, because agency is logically untenable. (1.316)

For that which is called its agency, being something additional to its nature as consciousness, would impart insentience to it, because of the consequence that there would be an excess over consciousness. (1.317)

"Surely the agency of primordial nature (prakṛti) is merely figuratively attributed to the person (puruṣa); this is sung in vain within the home by those who have strayed from the path of logic. (1.318)
For metaphorical usage does not establish the actual reality of things; let it be merely a designation devoid of such an object—so much for that. (1.319)
Even when designated by the metaphorical term "fire," a human being cannot dispel the cold arising from snowdrifts, spray, rain, and wind.
And for the Puruṣa who is the seer, Prakṛti is not proclaimed to be the seer; nor is there any other miserable being besides him who could metaphorically possess the status of an agent. (1.321)
Furthermore, what is the purpose of that [designation]? It arises from the conventional usage of agency;
however, a designation is not capable of altering the underlying reality. (1.322)
Even those who consider themselves experts in policy and have approached [us] regarding the agent, they too must first address this question presented by our intellect.
How can that agency which is established in the world through the performance of action and consists of vibration be applicable to the All-pervasive One, who is devoid of vibration? (1.324)
But surely, the triad of qualities—knowledge, the desire to act, and effort—inheres [in the self]; that which belongs to it therein is what has been cited as its agency. (1.325)
In this way, the intellect of those with childish minds might be deceived by impostors;
or even children might know [objects], were they not devoid of sensation. (1.326)
In that regard, knowledge is not the state of being an agent, since it exists everywhere; for desire and effort also generally exist for everyone and in all respects. (1.327)
Even if a potter, his mind tormented by the absence of a home, were to know [how to build one], desire it, and exert effort, what could he do? He would not have a house for himself. (1.328)
But surely he does not know how to build; therefore he does not desire to build; and because of that, he does not strive to build—how then can he have a house built? (1.329)

If the very form "to do" (kartum) is indeed the qualifier of knowledge and the other [mental states], then what would be the meaning of the root *kṛ* there, if it were supposedly characterized by vibration (*saspandatā*)? 1.330
Then one might say, "He knows how to move" or "He desires to move";
yet that movement belongs to his own self, not to him [the individual], because of the emergence of his sovereign power (*vaibhava*).
No other unshakable knowledge could possibly exist even for Śiva;
moreover, it has been stated that his instrument consists of the possession of knowledge, will, and effort. (1.332)
Regarding the phrase "to act for oneself," when one discriminates its meaning, one knows, desires, exerts effort, strives to know, endeavors to strive, and seeks to desire. (1.333)
The meaning of "each one" is expressed by the word "he knows how to act";
this would be the state of desiring to act, but it would not be the state of being the actual agent. (1.334)
If that were the case, verbal and bodily actions would become identical to mental ones; or else, how could his agency ever accrue through verbal and bodily actions? (1.335)
How can it be said that even mental actions belong to him, given the presence of the three qualities (guṇas) within the mind, speech, and body? 1.336

If it is argued that this [person] is a "partaker of karma" because of the accumulation of karmas, surely this would be a mere metaphorical designation; and it has already been explained that such a designation refers to something that is not a real entity. (1.337)

Furthermore, when other substances and qualities such as the soul's magnitude (mahattva) are present, since those [qualities] exist [in them], would that [soul] also become the locus of agency? (1.338)
Nor should one accept that [the self] exists [in liberation], for it would persist even in liberation; since this same rule applies equally when other qualities of the self are in proximity. (1.339)
Therefore, [if there were no self], there would be the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done;
moreover, since everything everywhere depends upon an intelligent being, what would be the use of a Lord? (1.340)

If causality is attributed [to the potter] in a task that exceeds mere spatial arrangement, while [the effect] is already fully completed by its own respective parts of inherence and other causal factors,
then what portion remains for the potter and others to attain such that they may possess the status of a cause?
For there does not exist even a fraction or a trace of that [defect] with respect to the creator of all.
Since there is no cognition, desire, or effort, and no agency other than these, therefore agency can never belong to anything else. (1.343)
They know that even for one who is a lord, sovereignty and agency derive from the Lord; thus, although there is a difference among the supreme lords, their natures remain identical. (1.344)
Actions do not have the inherent power to bind by their own nature; therefore, this [result], whether auspicious or inauspicious, must arise from that [action]. (1.345)
That sovereignty belongs to this Supreme Lord alone; this has been determined elsewhere by me myself, as it has been set forth in detail.
Therefore, enough; let us speak of the subject at hand: this supreme power of action is proclaimed as the "non-terrible" (aghoratva) aspect of the Lord for that very reason. (1.347)
For this very reason, there is courtesy toward these entities when they take refuge in Śiva;
for this is the direct path, and whatever action [is performed] is not devoid of its own essence.
"Surely there are no entities here that abide in Śiva-nature as agents. To this, he should respond: "True; however, being thus instructed, one should understand as follows: (1.349)
The God of gods is likewise devoid of the path of conceptualization regarding space, time, action, and agent; such is his power, which takes on every form.
That entire universe, though free from the slightest stain of the impurity of time and other such factors,
exists in non-difference from Bhairava.

Due to its sovereignty, that [consciousness] is sovereign; it remains surging within itself, and because it shines forth from there, it is also excluded from the penetration of Śiva, who has set. (1.352)
For this very reason, she is the supreme Dakṣiṇā, whose form is not terrible, as will be stated: "She bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva upon the circle of living beings. (1.353)

The knowers of that [reality] have declared the other non-terrible (aghorā) powers of Śiva to be supreme; moreover, elsewhere it is taught that the power of action (kriyāśakti) of Śiva resides within bound souls (paśu).

Binding [the breath], established in its own path, and known as the bringer of accomplishment, that expansion which is proclaimed as beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Ha'—[that is she]. (1.355)
That very [Bindu], having resorted to the state of being without vowels from its abode in Bindu, through the unfolding of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), becomes this entire garland of phonemes.
She remains indeed in the form of the reflective awareness "I have embraced [her]"; from that, there is the radiant flash of the full supreme ego-sense (pūrṇaparāhaṃkāra).
He is the devourer of the multitude of bound souls beginning with Ananta and ending with Viriñca,
having drawn into the cavern of his own belly the entire collection of the moving and unmoving worlds.

As long as the mass of individual souls (pudgala) is swallowed within the reflective awareness of one's own consciousness, for that long it exists in the form of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). // 1.359 //

[He is] whose state is adorned with inconceivable and innumerable varieties, and whose nature is distinguished by the peaceful and fierce aspects of infinite activities such as pacification and so forth. // 1.360 //
Moreover, due to the propriety of his well-established state, which was manifested by the greatness of his own absorption, even the various forms of Bhairava’s splendor [arose]. // 1.361 //
Variegated by the return to both the empty and the full states of existence,
they are solely intent upon devouring their own portion, known as the universe, which is the very nature of Śakti.
The powers (śaktis), cultivated by uprooting states that have long been established in the world and in time, [manifest] their own respective clusters of rays through their own expansion.

By relying on the reality of the truth of their resolve, they extended [their hands], which were appropriate for themselves, since they were excluded from the worldly conduct of the wicked. // 1.364 //
The scriptures indeed bring together [the teachings] that have reached full completion, just as they were when first produced within the sphere of transcending the world. (1.365)
In this context, that very conduct becomes the state in which all distinctions have been swallowed;
here stands the full Great Creation of the Supreme Lord.
In which [state] all those portions of dissolution and creation reside in the middle, it would not even be possible to say that she is merely the primordial creation. (1.367)
For how could there be the occurrence of "first" and so forth in reality, which is devoid of space and time?
This waking state is the primary one, participating in the stage of unfolding. (1.368)
This Brahmā, whose lotus-seat awakens him through a portion of his own power,
[manifests] these [powers], beginning from the form of Śiva and ending with that of Brahmā.
The powers of the Lord of Consciousness manifest by assuming forms;
even if it were possible to say, "This deity is only this much," [it would still be insufficient]. (1.370)
Because the Great Lord, whose nature is consciousness, is immeasurable, it was not clearly stated by me within the *Prabodhapañcadaśikā*. (1.371)
It has been stated that limited luminosity is indeed the defining characteristic of the insentient; for consciousness, being distinct from the insentient, is not so measured. (1.372)
Nevertheless, such a god himself, though devoid of human form,
by virtue of his own sovereignty, made himself both the moving and the unmoving.
By those born from Īśa and Tatpuruṣa— whether arisen, about to arise, or desiring to arise— individually, by groups of six, or by a single triad.
By means of three [factors] consisting of two natures. // 1.374 //
Thus, the manifold state of the ten divisions of Śiva arises precisely from the various consciousnesses through the power of their mutual intermingling. (1.375)
Even here in this [reality] called Śiva, diverse cognitions of duality were produced when there was a conjunction of the three faces—the left and the right. (1.376)
Then, through the future and present manifestations of each individual power, there is a triad of six; thus, by the division of Rudra, he is established as eighteenfold. (1.377)
Since each individual face is proclaimed to have five faces,
there is consequently an incalculable number of divisions arising from the eighteen-fold distinctions.
Since those [beings] are determined therein as being variegated by their respective previously mentioned cognitions and karmas, there is therefore no tautology.
For indeed, awakening, conduct, and the sequence of ritual action are each distinct, as they have been taught in various places; yet all [of them] lead to the abode of Śiva.
Just as all droplets of water find their rest in the great ocean, so too do all acts of knowledge and action find their rest in the Great Lord, the ocean of consciousness.
It is said that even the limited water on earth is drunk up by the rays of the sun,
and yet it returns again through the medium of rain to the great ocean; likewise,
every action and knowledge in this world clearly proceeds from itself.
Moreover, some others sink into the ocean of Śiva through traditional succession.
And that supreme heart-center (*hārda*) *liṅga* which is at the end on the right, considered to be the heart, is also completely filled with all the created states contained within it. (1.383)

And because it swallows the portions of light belonging to the illusory power that produces differentiation, it is black by virtue of being the destroyer of all things, assuming the form of darkness. (1.384)
For this very reason, it is stated in the Vijñānaśāstra by the Great Lord:
"The entire void is dissolved in the head," and so forth; such is the darkness of the All-pervasive One. (1.385)
In this very way, when the dark fortnight has arrived during the terrible night, one should meditate for a long time upon the form of Bhairava, which is difficult for those who meditate to overcome.

And it has been said: "Where there is suffering or darkness in a state devoid of duality, there is no connection with ignorance or karma, because one perceives dependence and other such conditions. (1.387)
Therefore, within this terrifying form that has the appearance of darkness, the four faces shine forth clearly through their internal absorption. 1.388
Desiring to emerge, it has thus emerged; desiring to become concealed, it is concealed.
Therefore, all at once, this [reality] consists of sixteenfold divisions.
The scripture consisting of sixty-four parts, known as Bhairava, entered simultaneously into Dakṣa, Vaisargika, Hārda, Svatantra, and Śiva. 1.390.
Thus, the Tantra known as Rudra, Śiva, and Bhairava exists in three ways;
for in reality, this very essence of knowledge unfolds in these three forms.

Through differentiation, through both difference and non-difference, and through the full union of non-difference, there likewise arise the three primary powers of Śambhu, beginning with Will (icchā). // 1.392 //
In that very context, however, through further elaboration, there is the conjunction with the five powers and so forth;
thus, in the middle, that Trika alone is differentiated, and likewise supreme.
This scripture has been preserved in our teacher’s house through the sequence of oral tradition;
for this very reason, due to its proximity, it encompasses both the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa scriptures.
The Kaulikī [power] unfolds at the edge of the limit of the Dhārā;
even beyond that, she is utterly full, having withdrawn all limiting adjuncts of phenomenal existence.

Bhairava, whose functional state is expanded by the surging flow of the ultimate reality, abides having embraced the three powers— Īśāna, Vāma, and Dakṣa— in their respective order, from the lower (apara) up to the limit of the supreme (parā). // 1.396 //
It manifests that differentiation of distinctions, brings about its clarity, and then, as the form of the Supreme Lord, is intent on swallowing that infinite [universe].
In reality, however, it is Triśiras alone who is without a rival. // 1.397 //
The Tantras and Kulas of the Upper [Tradition], the Left, and those other than them,
are established within this stream for the sake of abandoning the contraction of duality.

This very [reality], which is the object of illumination by another, consists of three aspects and is established in a threefold manner; it has been proclaimed by the Supreme Lord under the name Jñānacandra. (1.399)
All this meaning of the treatise is dependent upon the functioning of another's speech, in which distinctions such as the expressed and the expresser do not manifest. (1.400)

But afterwards, when the Self has manifested through the predominance of the aspect of the power of knowledge within the extremely subtle power of action, which is the perfection of sovereignty known as Sādākhya; 1.401.

Through the yoga of the manifestation of internal discourse within the locus of the intermediate [level] of speech (madhyamā), she exists in the form of phonemes, appearing as the nature of words and sentences. (1.402)
In the Svacchanda Śāstra, it is stated that the Lord Sadāśiva himself composed the Tantra by means of words consisting of preceding and succeeding phrases. (1.403)

And likewise, it is stated in that very same place regarding the enclosure of Suśiva: "In the path of the enclosure of Suśiva, which is prior [to the enclosure of Śiva], Sadāśiva is to be known there. (1.404)
Endowed with the ten Śivas and accompanied by the eighteen Rudras, his authority resides in the principle of Īśa; however, his desire to grasp that [higher state] lies in the principle of Śiva.

In the *varaṇa* [sheath], there is the supreme triad within the principle of power (*śaktitattva*) belonging to the pervasive Lord known as Bhairava, who is consciousness, arising from the point (*bindu*) in the abode of enjoyment (*bhogadhāman*) and from His manifestation (*vibhava*). (1.406)
Therefore, in the venerable Svacchanda-śāsana, it is stated that the state of Sthiti is above Īśvara and below the plane of Sadāśiva, within the enclosure of Suśiva. (1.407)
Immediately after that, among these various divisions of Śiva and Rudra established on the path of Māyā, the one called Śiva was spoken of by the Śivas. (1.408)
The division known as the Rudras attains a state of manifold variety through the gradual manifestation of the essence of emerging creative activity; thus it becomes clearly evident. (1.409)

The meanings of the scriptures, which pertain to the world, consist of phonemes, sentences, and words; they rely upon the illusory nature of all objects of perception and the diversity of heard speech. (1.410)
Depending upon them, those various introducers of the Tantras proceed;
therefore, first [one enters] as far as the cave of the illusory *vaikharī* speech. (1.411)

This meaning of the scripture, which is composed of illusory letters, has not arrived; it is merely a description consisting of supreme speech whose sole purpose is to awaken the inner essence. (1.412)

The meaning of the scriptures, ending with the worldly [level], is refined by the impressions rooted in the unartificial supreme entry; it exists within the thirty-seventh, the supreme, all-pervading [state].
For there is no reality whatsoever in things that do not exist; how can there be discipline when the master's nature is overcome by lack of discipline? (1.414)
Therefore, the entire meaning of all scriptures abides as the nature of the supreme reality;
consequently, even these [scriptures] such as the Vedas are but portions of the teaching belonging to Māyā.
They manifest solely through the power of Bhairava-Sūrya and not from anything else;
for indeed, there can never be any cause other than the reflective awareness of consciousness (saṃvid-vimarśa). (1.416)
The consciousness of the Lord of Consciousness is indeed consciousness itself, since it is precisely because of this nature that both effect and cause are metaphorically designated as such. (1.417)
For when an entity whose nature is to expand undergoes transformation, it is consciousness itself that appears as its form at both the beginning and the end. (1.418)
If consciousness could endure the reckoning of time,
then we would clearly be eating fragments of the moon from the sky, severed by a sharp sword.
Therefore, because consciousness does not deviate from its nature as pure awareness and because it is self-luminous, all scriptures are in reality self-luminous. (1.420)
Nor should it be said that [the denotatum] ever exists separately from the denoter, because the denoter itself exists independently as that which will become the denotatum. (1.421)
Sometimes the expressive element appears with its own form grasping the expressed object, while at other times it appears as the expressive element manifesting the universal.

Never indeed does [the object] appear as qualified by proximate or infinite qualifiers, but rather it shines forth through the predominance of its own manifest essential nature and its denotable aspect. // 1.423 //

Therefore, there is sometimes intent upon the meaning and likewise intent upon the form; in some cases, it is intent upon the object desired to be known, while in others, it is a state consisting of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (1.424)
Since consciousness never departs from its own nature, it is observed as the manifold form of words;
what wonder is there that consciousness shines forth through these various expressions? (1.425)
Thus, sound is non-different from the state of reflective awareness whose essence is Śiva; because it is manifest, it illuminates both itself and others here,
