and that alone— pure reflective awareness, the very core of consciousness— is the means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, that other [designation] is due to the power of metaphorical designation; for it is thus: (1.426)
This ultimate consciousness, which is self-luminous by nature, is called self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), from which the entire order of the universe is established. (1.427)
And this very [power] does not transcend the essential nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa); reflective awareness is its supreme, full enjoyment, which is designated as Paśyantī. (1.428)

It should be understood that this very Goddess is both transcendent and immanent (parāparā), designated as "Māna" (the means of knowledge), wherein the object of knowledge (meyam) residing in the immanent aspect is established through identity. 1.429.
For there can be no determination of the object of measurement by means of a distinct instrument of knowledge;
indeed, the crow cannot claim whiteness simply because the swan is white. (1.430)

And thus the Guru Śaṅkaranandana has said this very thing: "It is not [established] because of its being a means of valid cognition, nor because it is other than that, nor because of sublation; there is no stability in what lacks stability. (1.431)

An entity does not attain proof as an external existence through properties that are inseparable from manifestation and whose nature is restricted to its being; therefore, it is not an [external] entity. (1.432)
Therefore, consciousness itself, in assuming the states of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge, shines by its very nature as self-luminous. (1.433)

And that [consciousness], beautiful with the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the word whose essence is the mantra abiding within it, is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by itself alone, because it does not depend on anything else. (1.434)
The proponents devised various names for her through many figurative turns of expression, all of which arose solely from her grace.
And so, that which has been proclaimed—that perception is established by the chisel of the circle of the sense-faculties such as the eye—is now being analyzed. (1.436)

If the determination of the sense-faculties were not distinct from consciousness, then there would be no unity of object and means of cognition, just as in the case of external objects such as jars and the like. (1.437)

Now, the eyes and other such organs are instruments for the self, not for jars and the like; therefore, the measurement of entities occurs by means of those [organs] alone, and not by means of jars and so forth. (1.438)

Furthermore, if this [air], which is considered all-pervasive, were to come into contact [with the sense organs] without distinction, then because there is no difference in its being composed of the elements (bhautikatva), it would [contact] the eyes and other senses just as it does with jars and the like. (1.439)
How could the fulfillment of the self’s requirement for an instrument be certain? A specific conjunction alone is the basis for being an instrument. (1.440)
The distinction [between them] arises from those various actions proclaimed as dharma and adharma;
this very [distinction] consists of the manifestation of the existence of logical reasoning. (1.441)
Speaking thus, he deceives the simple-minded while being intent on flight;
for [he denies] that which arises from the power of a self that pervades all conjunctions of the senses.
It is called "mind" (manas) because it simultaneously cuts off [the flow of] cognition;
regarding that as well, we say that first the self alone is joined with the mind. (1.443)

In that case as well, let it be considered who would effect the conjunction of the self and the mind; for if it were [the self] due to its omnipresence, then the mind would encounter all [selves] at once. (1.444)

If the internal organ, acting as the presiding controller, were to depend upon the eyes and other sense organs, then upon the conjunction of even one [organ], everyone would attain omniscience. (1.445)
Therefore, the locus of objects [is perceived] through as many portions of the sense-faculties as there are;
it is illuminated by contact with those subtle portions of parts that are situated within the sense-faculty. (1.446)
Even if a single atom of an external object, such as a sacrificial pit, were to appear, provided it has been brought into the range of the senses through the influence of the mind; 1.447.
In that case, its very capacity regarding its own object arises; thus, the rays of the eyes emerge through even the most subtle apertures.
Why do they not exercise valid cognition regarding the flood of entities that exist everywhere?
For surely, the sense organs are fully capable of apprehending those entities situated within their appropriate range. (1.449)
Indeed, let the nature of the fitness of a location be investigated:
that place where one who is situated therein attains cognition is said to be fit. (1.450)
"Wherein situated would cognition exist?"—why is this not demonstrated?
Thus, these who fancy themselves logicians are devoid of the presentation of valid reasoning. (1.451)

Why did he not remain silent from the very beginning? What is the use of these boastful claims, since this [confrontation] has occurred by force against one whose own intentions have been rendered fruitless?
Could the conjunction of the mind with the sense-organ not be improper? Or rather, does an intention toward an object arise for it? (1.453)
If [the object] is unknown, what intention could there be? If it is known, what is the purpose of the contact with the sense-faculties?
And if it is already clearly perceived, why would it need to be remembered, given that the intention has already been cultivated by the agent? (1.454)
The effort of one who intends toward one thing arises in relation to another;
[these efforts] are dependent upon the sense organs, such as the eye, which are connected to the mind and linked to the self. (1.455)
How could objects, by the process of transcending the eyes and other senses that have become their immediate conditions, extend the state of being a knower within the Self alone? (1.456)

But surely, the status of being a cognizer is produced by cognition; since that cognition inheres in the self, how can there be any suspicion of the status of a cognizer in anything other than that? (1.457)
"We say that this very thing is knowledge; how could it be otherwise?"—out of fear, he who was blinded by partiality for his own side offered this very same reply. (1.458)
Just as the mind is said to be the cause for the conjunction of the sense organ and the self, so too let another cause be stated for the conjunction of the self and the mind. (1.459)

If that were the case, there would be an infinite regress, which would undermine the very foundation [of the argument]; therefore, the conjunction of the self with its own internal organ must be accepted as being eternal.
Those who are always asleep, intoxicated, unconscious, or wretched would be knowers;
yet such knowledge is not desired by you, as it is for the disciples of the Śākya. (1.461)
Therefore, how can that which is called "perceptibility" be other than the range of the sense organs?
Now, an examination of each of these will be set forth in detail. (1.462)
In that regard, the mind is minute, eternal, all-pervading, swift, light, and non-material; yet even this [mind] does not attain the status of being established by logical reasoning here.
If the mind were atomic and moved so swiftly that it could repeatedly touch objects, then at that very moment, the body would become a corpse.

Even when the mind is situated within the body, because of the application of knowledge directed toward that very [Self], the individual soul (jīva) would become a mere single atom; the remainder would be like a jar or a wall. (1.465)
Now, if a connection with one's own internal organ (svānta) has arisen anywhere within the sphere of the self,
then that knowledge of the pervasive self (vibhu-ātman) is its inherent property (samavāyin), and thus it possesses the status of being a knower.
If [the soul] is "born," why is the life-force residing in all bodies not established?
By this very logic, why would there not be a life-force even for a jar or similar objects? (1.467)
For when knowledge arises within the self as a manifestation, it exists there in a partial manner;
however, when it resides again within the mind alone, its existence would be composed of parts, confined to the mere body. (1.468)
If the mind were omnipresent, there would be simultaneous cognition of everything; and if the mind were eternal, knowledge would therefore exist at all times. (1.469)
Even the state of liberation arises only for one who possesses the yoga of consciousness; that there is no conjunction of the self and the mind in liberation—this is truly marvelous. (1.470)
For how could the pervasiveness of one's own self be obstructed in liberation? And if it were non-material, how could the mind be directed toward all objects? (1.471)
Since the luminous nature of the eye is indeed accepted solely because of its skill in manifesting specific objects, why is the mind not likewise considered material? (1.472)
If the mind were capable of apprehending all objects, what would be the use of the other elaborate sense organs?
Surely, regarding its external object, the sense organ has utility prior [to the operation of the mind]. (1.473)

For instance, regarding the subsequent state of the mind when an object is perceived by a sense faculty, it is said here that it is just as [the object] was not previously grasped by the sense faculty. (1.474)
If that is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then what need is there for subsequent mental engagement?
But if it is merely a universal (*sāmānyamātra*), then that was already grasped previously by the sense faculties. (1.475)
And at that time, since there is no determination of the individual by means of the mind, how could there be a grasping of the universal by the mind? (1.476)
How can there be a perception of a universal without the perception of the individual?
Furthermore, if there were such a perception of a universal, its capacity to refer to all things would be contradicted. (1.477)
Regarding that object which has been described as being devoid of the apprehension of specific qualities and as the total negation of all words, its quality of "swift movement" [is asserted]. (1.478)
How can the act of going be exactly the same in the case of one's own hand situated in front, a jar located some distance away, and Mount Meru which is extremely far off? (1.479)
Because, among those things that move swiftly, a distinction is perceived based on their proximity or lack thereof to the previously existing light, wherever it may be. (1.480)
And how could it perceive non-material, subtle things such as mountains?
Manifestation is brought about by that which is similar through that which is similar. (1.481)
Granted that the primordial intellect (buddhi) arises first, from which comes the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛt), and from that the mind (manas);
even so, the atomicity of the mind is not at all established.
The previously mentioned objections remain valid by virtue of their pervasiveness; enough with these logical arguments for our purpose of winning over the mind. (1.483)
Just as it is desired by those with views deluded by duality through other systems of thought,
so too does the light of the conscious self partake in such an appearance.
Let that power be the mind, fashioned by its own autonomy; wherever there is the auditory organ and space, there the hearing of all sounds occurs. (1.485)

Since space is everywhere unobstructed by the eyes and other sense organs, any obstruction caused by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) is invalidated by the presentation of logical reasoning. (1.486)

How could deafness and the like occur, or how could their medical treatment be possible? [The answer is: through the impairment of the support for the binding [of consciousness], there is likewise the favoring of that [consciousness]. (1.487)
The sense organ [the eye] inheres only in its own constituent parts; as for space, it is established that it is not at all dependent on anything as a substratum. (1.488)
But as for its being conjoined, it exists together with existence;
therefore, let it undergo modification through the favoring or harming of that [existence]. (1.489)
"That which is the favor is the favor; it has that as its basis"—this construction of our own words appears to us as utterly devoid of substance. 1.490
When it is urged, "Clearly state that the favoring of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*) occurs by way of their basis; what, then, is the basis for these? (1.491)

The principle that "that which is the application of its assistance is itself the substratum" does not escape being a circular argument (*cakraka*), as these factors mutually depend upon one another. (1.492)
That which was called the tactile sense, whose nature is wind, is now analyzed:
the state of wind is established as being possessed of velocity and unobstructed. (1.493)
Then, what is the sequence [of reasoning] that [establishes] "touch" occurs in the location of the body and not in a wall?
Furthermore, the visual organ is composed of fire (*taijasa*), and its light has extended toward the external object. (1.494)
It is now being examined how it is known that objects have form as their primary quality;
for if that light is invisible, how could it be impelled by the mind? (1.495)
For an impulse that is not accompanied by cognition can never occur; nor is the visual light ever known by the sense organ itself. (1.496)
Furthermore, for you, the mind is not independent regarding what is known by the sensory faculties; and if it were unimpelled, it would perceive everything, in every way, and at all times. (1.497)
There would indeed be an inconsistency regarding either its engagement in activity or its cessation;
moreover, if that light were merely the shape of the eyeball, [it would not illuminate]. (1.498)
To that extent, there would be apprehension only of what is situated therein and not of anything else anywhere; yet this is the opposite even when the eyeball is closed. (1.499)
Or rather, when the eye is opened and the circle of rays has spread forth, there would be a perception of every object everywhere. (1.500)

For him, there is no conventional reality as there is for one looking at a cloth; therefore, when the eyes are closed, why would there not be a perception of the object by one whose eyes are shut? (1.501)
In the midst of thick darkness, for one whose eyes are closed, there appears a manifestation of variegated light, even though the pair of eyes is oppressed by it. (1.502)
How could yogins perceive a *bindu* in the darkness? Or how could that [perception] occur even when the eyes are opened? For there is never any apprehension of a real object [in such cases]. (1.503)
By means of mental superintendence, there is an expansion exceeding that of an atom; why is that dependence upon a lamp not also contradicted? (1.504)
The light of a lamp assists the internal self, the eyes, and the objects; if it were so for every mental modification, then there would be a latent impression (saṃskāra) for each one. (1.505)
If a lamp were being conceptualized at night, there would be the apprehension of its form;
this would be so if the self were subject to refinement, because of its omnipresence.
Since conjunction and refinement would result in the cognition of form at all times, what other kind of refinement can be said to exist for that which is formless and eternal? (1.507)
If it is an aid to the eye, then a form situated in the midst of light would never appear when the rays are located at the region of the eye. (1.508)

Now, [it may be argued: "Surely that multitude of ocular rays reaches the location of the object; alas, why then does consciousness not arise in that very place, rather than in the location of the self? (1.509)

Since the self exists as omnipresence in that very [body] and the instruments [of perception] exist in that very place, therefore the claims that "the body is the locus of experience" or "it is the living being" are mere empty words. (1.510)
When the movement of the rays of the eyes has been determined, [the path] in the unobstructed forest track is clearly perceived from one's own hand onwards. (1.511)
How indeed could the perception of the sun, moon, and so forth arise, since even when they move swiftly, the aforementioned distinction between being distant and not distant persists? (1.512)

When that [object] is obscured by the illumination of a lamp or the eye, how could cognition be pure regarding an entity that has come under the influence of those two [defects], such as discoloration? (1.513)
Blindness and its medical treatment would not be possible if there were a corruption of the locus;
furthermore, if the tongue were of the nature of water, then that water would flow away from it.
Then how can there be stability for it? And what is the manifestation of various flavors for that which, in its union with a single flavor, abides in a state of non-dual flavor? (1.515)
There would be no cognition of a single taste; just as when there is an excess of bile, the function of the tongue perceives bitterness and sweetness is not known—so it is with patience. (1.516)

[Objection: "But the pungency residing in bile is not like that which has reached the tongue; therefore, bile and the hidden [object] are equal insofar as they both travel along the path of the tongue. (1.517)
Thus, there would be a simultaneous cognition of both bitterness and sweetness;
if the tongue were devoid of taste, how could it manifest flavors? (1.518)
If you say it is due to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then what is this insistence on its being watery?
And since the nose is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), why is its solidity not perceived? (1.519)
Now, one might object: "In that which is characterized by an excess of the quality of fragrance, does that fragrance not manifest?
Is there no such valid cognition [of it] when the sense organ is present and the fragrance is manifested? (1.520)
There exists indeed a mind that is odorless, not of the nature of earth, yet capable of apprehending odors; therefore, an inference based on such [a mind] is not possible for you. 1.521.

Therefore, it is not tenable that the aggregate of the senses is composed of the elements; rather, if they are derived from the ego-principle (ahaṃkārika), their nature as pervaders and their non-differentiation [from the source] are established. (1.522)
Furthermore, there is a contradiction regarding the body as a substratum, and there is no persistence [of the self] by way of being an instrument;
let that pentad of organs of action, beginning with speech, be examined. (1.523)
That particular essence of speech, which arises from the impact of the vital breath (samīra) extending from the navel to the crown of the head, is described here as being of such a nature. (1.524)
Sound would be its effect; let it be considered who the agent here might be.
The self possesses no agency at all, even if that were the case, because of its omnipresence. (1.525)
When the sound has been uttered by me, why do you not become the speaker?
This defect exists even in the primordial nature (prakṛti); the agent is devoid of agency.
There is no stability for the instrument; since the vocal organ is the same [in all cases], how is it that the state of being indistinct or perfectly clear arises in sounds? (1.527)
And how could there be a distinction residing in the sound during whispered conversation, recollection, and so forth, if it were due to effort?
If that effort also [merely] arises [from another cause], then how [could it produce such a distinction]? (1.528)

For indeed, a distinct [result] arises, since the production of qualities from something else does not occur; by means of which [result], the [defect] is counteracted through the intensity or mildness of the effort. (1.529)
And since the sense-faculty of the hand does not take [an object], how could there be grasping by means of the mouth and so forth?
Furthermore, if "appropriation" (svīkāra) is what you intend by "grasping," what indeed is that appropriation? (1.530)
The making of one's own is called "appropriation" (*svīkāra*);
and if the word *sva* denotes the self (*ātman*), then in that case, the self would be [identified with] primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (1.531)
Therefore, since there is nothing whatsoever that is non-ordinary, how indeed can there be a lack of self-mastery?
Furthermore, if the ego were the self, then the act of "I-making" would not exist in a jar. (1.532)
"This belongs to me"—by this very [notion], it is refuted;
for everything that is related to the ego-sense is indeed one's own. (1.533)
For the self, which is all-pervasive, there exists neither anything of its own nor anything that is not its own;
such is the equal application of this logical principle to the sense organ of the foot as well. (1.534)

Furthermore, that which is called "going" by virtue of reaching another place from one place is established as being of the nature of abandonment, precisely through the absence of appropriation. (1.535)
This act of acceptance is also refuted; even regarding that aspect of acceptance which occurs in motion, the hand is the appropriate instrument, not that which is called the foot. (1.536)
For in this way, a confusion of the functions of the sense-faculties arises with respect to their respective objects;
for this very reason, by those who know the great system of logic, it is held as the final view. (1.537)
A great deal of elaborate virtuous speech has been uttered to prohibit motion:
"That which has already gone is not being traversed, and that which has not yet gone is certainly not being traversed. (1.538)
In one's own system, that which is free from coming and going does not exist, and so forth; furthermore, the anal faculty is not merely a cavity, due to the movement of the abdominal wind. (1.539)
Indeed, its abandonment would result in confusion; therefore, such a state of affairs would exist.
That which is called the organ of generation and its function—[it is said that] it ceases;
thus, the status of inference as a means of valid cognition is not tenable.
For those who maintain that there is a distinction between them, two means of valid cognition are certainly not compatible. (1.604)
But for sound and the like, it has been thoroughly determined by the wise through inference;
therefore, this [consciousness] exists as self-awareness alone, by virtue of its self-luminosity. (1.605)

This luminous manifestation shines forth through the manifold elaborations of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; it is a light like the moon, possessing the grace of thick waves upon the ocean,
and acting as the companion that causes the buds of night-lotuses to burst open.

That expansion of supreme consciousness which occurs through the intermingling of the means of knowledge, the object, and the knower—this is the manifold art of conceptualization in the world. (1.606)
Therefore, this very Light, perfectly replete with manifold powers, shines by itself in diverse forms everywhere and in every way. (1.607)

Therefore, this [cognition] which possesses a clear manifestation through the medium of worldly forms and so forth, receives the designation "perception" (pratyakṣa) due to a portion of its own power arising from what is called conceptual construction (vikalpa). (1.608)

For thus it is: that [state] is the unfolding of the vision which is a portion of the God of gods; it is the vibration of the vital breath; it is one-pointedness; it is being; it is the accumulation of its qualities.
Thus, all that appears in this manner is clearly perception;
however, in this case, there is no application of categories such as agent, object, or instrument. (1.610)
Surely this [consciousness] exists in the Western path of conceptualization, because the appearance of the body and the jar is initially clear, whereas subsequently it becomes unclear. (1.611)

That very same [consciousness], however, when its form is concealed, is the self-awareness of its own pure aspect; even there, in the manifestation of the body and the jar, this is precisely the same process.
Even in the manifestation of millions of bodies, up to a thousandfold, if there is no such expansion [of consciousness] therein, whether before or after, [it is not true manifestation]. (1.613)
It reaches the state of reflective awareness, variegated by being both distinct and indistinct;
yet it is that one alone whose nature is essentially manifest. (1.614)
The light of Śiva emerges.
This diversity does not exist in reality; rather, diversity is conceptualized there through the immersion into that which is not of its own nature. (1.615)
Furthermore, entry into a form other than that [of Śiva] within the light of Śiva is not logical; or rather, by the force of the reasoning already stated, there is no diversity anywhere. (1.616)
However, that which appears as variegated indeed produces a variegated state; thus, this Caitra, appearing to us like a variegated thing, is of such a nature. (1.617)
Enough with that opinion of Maitreya; he who sees me as one who perceives existence, while being seen by me, is one who is fully established in meditative concentration.
Indeed, in previous tens of millions of births, he experienced various sufferings and the like;
yet even one who has come by this path shall be liberated through meditative practice and other means.
Even that other [subject] who possesses liberation arises in this way without end; yet this light is truly one, which for a long time has not been divided.
For this very reason, there is no duality whatsoever that could truly grasp Maheśvara, who is non-dual and beautiful with light and bliss. (1.621)

If place, time, form, cognition, properties, limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and so forth, which are accepted as differentiators, appear [as such], then that manifestation (*vibhā*) is likewise [of that nature]. (1.622)
If that [non-duality] is indeed such a non-distinction, then this non-duality is manifest; the word "distinction," however, is merely abandoned by conceptual cognition. (1.623)

Or let there be a conceptualization of difference that arises within the manifestation; nevertheless, by the logic already stated, it will find its firm foundation in that very [manifestation] itself. (1.624)
This is a jar and this is a cloth; these two are distinct from one another, they are distinct from other cognizers, and they are also distinct from me. (1.625)
Thus, this one Light is of the very nature of reflective awareness (amarśa).
[Objection: But if this is so, is this not a form of partiality? How can there be non-duality for you? (1.626)
Let there even be a distinction; why indeed is it not tolerated directly?
This is merely an attempt to encourage song and instrumental music among a gathering of deaf people. (1.627)
For we do not assert non-duality by means of subverting the penetration of duality; for that would indeed be an admission of your position, since duality would then be quite evident. (1.628)
"This is duality, this is not"—wherein both "this" and "that," as well as the pair of duality and non-duality, shine forth equally, that is declared to be non-duality. (1.629)
"Let it be so; we do not crave distinctions either.
Let that [distinction] exist, for it is neither to be rejected nor accepted by us, just as it is for you in this case. (1.630)
If you wish to embrace the side that benefits all beings,
then you should take refuge in the supreme non-dual vision as your great shelter.
This truth will be established in the eighteenth chapter; let that which is to be attained at the end be the ultimate reality from the perspective of the highest truth.
In this regard, those who have not found rest rely upon limited consciousness and are thus utterly subverted by the delusions arising from birth and death. (1.633)
Therefore, that very one, this single Light which is the Supreme Lord, is directly perceived; it shines by means of that very Light itself. 1.634
There, all those views necessarily enter like great rivers into the ocean; once they have entered, they proceed to the fulfillment of their purpose.
For instance, the causal complex of mental cognition arises together with its mother [the preceding moment of consciousness] and its object, or excluding those two, in many ways. (1.636)
And having known [the object], one causes the measure [of cognition] to proceed, yet one does not abandon the state of being a measure;
this conjecture regarding the basis of direct perception is now established. (1.637)
Moreover, since cognition apprehends what has not been previously known, this entire universe appears in various ways according to the power of Bhairava’s will. (1.638)
Manifesting the object and clearly effecting the engagement, it indeed causes that very object to be attained, by virtue of its being presented as appearing in such a manner. (1.639)

Even such cognitions as "this is exclusively existent" or "it is not non-existent" certainly appear from the perspective of ultimate reality; therefore, the vision of non-absolutism (anekānta) is clearly evident. 1.640.
A single entity has the nature of all entities,
and all entities have the nature of that single entity;
this is our well-observed doctrine of the Arhat.
And it is also stated in the Śrīsāraśāstra: "It is joined [with the breath]. (1.641)

"Who in this world is capable of determining the number or the essential nature of this world, such that 'this is the measure' and 'that is the measured'?"— even this [question] is considered true by the Lord of Speech, the Blessed One, who is blessed with the bliss of consciousness.
Since there is nothing else here besides this state of silence, what could anyone else possibly do? (1.642)
If an entity were to appear without a cause, there would be no restriction regarding its limited direction or time;
therefore, this restriction must arise from a cause. Whose greatness is this?
Is it the nature of the cause? If so, then why is that nature not manifested openly?
It is not said that the entity itself exercises control over another; for by what means could one thing govern another?
By its very nature, this Self is Supreme Śiva; such is the teaching of the Āgamas.
Defined as the Soul of the Universe, it unfolds within the entire world.
Therefore, let this consciousness of the elements be non-different from the earth and the rest.
It is barren with respect to space and time, being devoid of birth, death, and states of woe. // 1.644 //

Why does this grasping—that "this is his world" and "following that, this is the next world"—touch him? For time does not affect him; therefore, he possesses the majesty of supreme bliss, the essence of joy arising from absolute freedom.
He is blessed by the complete reduction to ashes of the entire flood of the bonds of impurity.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya perspective, which encompasses the entire range of principles, is here discussed at length; it is seen to extend sufficiently from the earth upward.
And that arises from the most subtle cause.
Furthermore, that which is intent upon performing grasping consists of ten external instruments;
its internal cause is threefold.
It is a mirror for the delusion regarding pleasure and pain. // 1.647 //
That which is likewise composed of the three qualities must,
moreover, because of its insentience and its state of differentiation,
depend upon a further ultimate cause.
This night is said here to be the object of enjoyment, and that [enjoyment] consists of dependence upon the enjoyer;
it does not mutually attain the status of being the enjoyer. (1.648)
Indeed, a single body cannot consist of both the enjoyed and the enjoyer due to their contradictory natures; therefore,
the enjoyer is merely the power of consciousness.
Therefore, by virtue of being composed of the nature of consciousness, the mind [is so]. 1.649.
How could the all-pervading Lord, who is omnipresent,
enter into the state of being an enjoyer associated with duality?
Therefore, [the world] is created by His own sovereign power.
One should resort to a state characterized by contraction and stability.
Because it lacks any other cause such as the kalās and so forth,
this is known as its innate impurity (sahaja-mala);
through its power, that [impurity] manifests in three ways.
This very one is declared to be that person. // 1.651 //
Because it is dependent upon the state of being the enjoyer,
this [limited subject] appears as having a covering (kañcuka) by way of necessary concomitance; thus, the knower of time [perceives] that it is not otherwise.
It is named "the restraint of passion. (1.652)
If this Self, moreover, by its own power fully reveals its own nature— which had been concealed by its unrestrained innate sovereignty— then, arising from that pure consciousness,
it indeed establishes agency and the entire range of effects within its own awareness.
Perceiving this, one who is firm in the thought "I am all this, existing eternally," shall attain lordship.

Because he perceives within his own consciousness— the consciousness whose vision flashes from within the heart— that the knower, when the object of knowledge appears clearly, undergoes a concealment of its difference [from it],
this [consciousness] swiftly attains both difference and unity between "this" and "I."
The cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) reveals the state belonging to Sadāśiva. // 1.654 //
All that is to be known and all effects are dissolved within awakening; as long as they remain there, they exist within the mass of the blazing flames of consciousness whose activity is overflowing.
That very expansion seems to cast off its own body. // 1.655 //
This sense of "this-ness" (idaṃbhāva), which was previously intent on dissolving, has not yet dissolved; even in its prior stage, it possessed the same luster, but now,
with the emergence of the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva), the manifestation of existence becomes boundless.
Thus, this supreme Śakti, known as Bhūriṣi, resides within her own perfected Self.

It strives to fall away from the subsequent [state], yet it falls there through the union of the preceding and succeeding forms; thus, being adorned by a manifold collection of consciousnesses, this entire ground is called Śākta. (1.657)
In each and every reality, the God of gods, assuming every stage according to his own will,
is the perfect single Self, whose very nature is perfect consciousness.
The illustrious Bhairava is thus defined in the Śāstra. (1.658)
This vision of the descent of power (śaktipāta) is described according to the divisions of weak, moderate, and extremely intense;
it is quite sufficient even with its various mutual subdivisions.
That which is the perception of the self's own nature. (1.659)
Now, does this Lord, who is perfect consciousness, ever manifest his own nature, or does he ever conceal it? For what indeed could be a causeless restriction? 1.660
It has indeed been stated previously that there is no other cause for the observances (niyamas) than the Infinite;
even in worldly matters, He alone is the Great Lord.
Having the nature of manifesting various and diverse appearances. // 1.661 //
Beyond that freedom, we shall not now utter further words.
Ascending the series of palatial waves of the celebrated ocean of consciousness, there is peace; following that, it is designated by the name "bondage."
Thus, liberation is that in which the flavor [of worldly existence] has been completely grasped in this manner, as previously described. (1.662)
Expressions such as "always," "at some time," "now," and "then" are conceptualizations of the play of time, which manifest through the absolute freedom of consciousness.
Nor is that Supreme Lord touched by the divisions of time,
for those divisions have no independent existence apart from the conceptualization of Him.
Therefore, even within the objective aspect created by Himself—which is His own essential nature—this appearance of dependence is clearly manifested by the Lord alone. (1.665)
The independent Supreme Lord exercises both dependence and independence; no other characteristic is said to exist apart from independence and dependence. (1.666)
For that which has limited manifestation is insentient; therefore, if that which stands here as the delimiting agent were also clearly a delimited object, [then it too would be insentient]. (1.667)
Therefore, when its form is being apprehended, the illumination does not manifest;
for in this way, the external objective portion does not manifest by itself. (1.668)
Knowledge has the nature of illuminating an object, yet it is indeed unmanifested; for its inherent substrate (the self) likewise does not shine by way of its own essential form. (1.669)
Even his sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, do not appear; and there is no appearance at all of light and the like apart from consciousness. (1.670)

If cognition has indeed arisen, then this luminosity of the object must be either its power or its property; if so, then omniscience would have been attained throughout the entire circle of the universe.

Now, that which is designated as "manifestation" is something entirely different; it is not connected at all to any of the categories of the object of knowledge, the knower, or the means of knowledge. (1.672)
Furthermore, this entire universe would always remain unmanifest, if there were a manifestation of an entity that is inherently non-luminous. (1.673)
By that much alone its own nature would be lost through diminution;
and if the manifestation of the arising of knowledge belongs to an entity that remains within its own nature, [then it must arise from itself]. (1.674)
Since the state of abiding in one's own nature is undifferentiated for the universe, why would that [consciousness] not belong to it?
Therefore, the manifestation of the universe is established as being based on its own delimitation.

If the delimiting subject, differentiated by the various forms arising from the manifestation of its own freedom, were thus itself to become the delimited object, then [the consequence would follow]. (1.676)
This infinite regress, which would destroy its own root, will fall away; therefore, that [cognition] is called "undetermined" while being the determiner. (1.677)
Therefore, it is not admissible in the treatises; thus, that [object] is not within the domain of time.
Consequently, its nature as an object of cognition has been defined as being beyond time.
If Time were to delimit the mother, then the stability of Time would certainly require that its own existence be supported by the mother alone. (1.679)
Furthermore, no other mother could possibly exist, as that would lead to an infinite regress; nor could this [person] approach to kill her, for she is devoid of temporal duration.
But if that very time which is the object to be delimited is indeed attached to the cognizer, then how, for you, can there be both the cognizer and the cognized in a single entity? (1.681)
For such is your settled conviction regarding the doctrine of difference;
however, for us who maintain the doctrine of non-difference, let there be no refutation whatsoever. (1.682)
For those for whom the universe consists of the Mother and the Mother likewise consists of the universe,
that Supreme Lord is not defiled by the mud of the web of temporal divisions.
For the light of the power of consciousness (citiśakti) indeed assumes impurity;
therefore, it is concealed at that time, and subsequently becomes manifest in form. (1.684)
Thus, this very yawning of his, which designates him as suchness, is a certain act of measurement (kalana) consisting of the self-reflection of his own nature. 1.685.
In that [state], he conceives of himself as a self worthy of the yoga of Śiva,
because through the application of manifold variety, he conceives of himself in such a way.
Therefore, he has stated here that the descent of power (śaktipāta) is established in nine ways; otherwise, there would be no passion or aversion in the Lord anywhere. (1.687)
By which means the omnipresent Lord causes his own inherent power to descend upon someone at any time;
such is this descent of power (śaktipāta) from the Great Lord, occurring without any external cause.

Therefore, through the exhaustion of passion, the balancing of karma, the weight of well-performed deeds, the ripening of impurities, association with friends, devotion, the state of being, and service; // 1.689 //

Through practice, through the breaking forth of latent impressions, through the ripening of mental formations, through the destruction of false knowledge, through the renunciation of karma, and through the cessation of desire for rewards; 1.690.
As for the claim that "that power falls from the mind due to equanimity," that is indeed false, for even in that case one must seek another cause. (1.691)
Because of the occurrence of infinite regress, over-extension, possibility, and impossibility, and because of the fall into mutual dependence, a ladder, a circle, and so forth; (1.692)
But in this position, the validity of all doctrines is established; for in this "all-enduring" position, nothing at all is found to be faulty. (1.693)
Since the wise can apply reasoning to this matter themselves, no separate application of it has been stated here.
That this [view] is extensive in its textual formulation is false. (1.694)
Therefore, they approached Śiva’s power, which is free from dependence; for without it,
the state of liberation would be in vain.
In other treatises, there are discourses concerning liberation.
O Lord, at the time of the descent of power (śaktipāta), You never engage in deliberation;
thus the venerable teacher Utpala has described it.
In various places within its own scripture, it is stated thus: // 1.696 //
For it is by His grace alone that devotion is produced in men, through which those whose minds are absorbed in His being attain the supreme perfection. (1.697)

Thus, in the Purāṇas, the Śāstras, and other such works, that power of the Supreme Lord is said to be entirely independent; for if it were dependent on anything else, He would lack sovereignty. (1.698)

Only by those whose sight is obscured and dulled by the blindness of the doctrine of duality is the incapacity of this [reality] for being restricted to any particular location invariably perceived. (1.699)
By incessantly deliberating upon such webs of causes as "the ripening of the equality of karmic impurities," one merely exhausts oneself in vain. (1.700)
That [dependence] is of no benefit to them, being like clutching at kusa and kāśa grass;
therefore, he alone is such [a master], augmented by his own sovereignty. (1.701)
Then, through various manifestations such as "thus" and "so," that [reality] appears;
in this way, all philosophical views converge right here within the Supreme Lord. (1.702)
Enough with these elaborate displays of reasoning by others regarding "entry";
thus has the nature of the God of gods been declared here. 1.703.
In that regard, some have maintained that direct perception is the sole authority, bearing the burden of all means of knowledge; indeed, such an authority is one alone. (1.704)

The inference "there is fire because of smoke" is generally just an expansion of that very [perception], just as [the cognition of] a jar is established solely based on the prior perception of its preceding parts. (1.705)
The mother [cognition], considering the mental cognition—which consumes the object in both its manifest and unmanifest forms—to be indeed manifest, attains the status of direct perception. (1.706)

Nor is there inference regarding the final part [of the object], because that consciousness is one and the same; for it is like the manifestation of fire, which is contained within the perceptual cognition of smoke. (1.707)

First of all, a cognition arises that grasps only a single portion of the object; let it be stated that perception is that [cognition] which possesses a clear form regarding that very portion. (1.708)

Just as there is a variety of jewels and so forth, so too is there a variety in consciousness regarding the eye, the self, the mind, light, objects, and the rest, due to the arrangement of their conditioning factors (saṃskāra). // 1.709 //
It appears with clarity as direct perception within consciousness itself, due to the persistence of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the locus of such a pervasion (*vyāpti*).
In the same way, that cognition previously appeared in the form of smoke and fire;
and just as firm latent impressions (saṃskāra) are vividly manifest, they suddenly appear of their own accord.
Those whose selves are hungry for enjoyment, being obscured by internal obstacles, perceive the reality of the jewels and so forth very quickly and with absolute certainty. (1.712)

Because one takes up food and so forth to eat without any intervention by [the senses] such as the pervasive [mind], that conceptual construction which others have asserted would be refuted thereby. (1.713)

For we do not consider that there is any need for a conceptual construction of pervasion regarding the cognition of the essential nature of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva-svabhāva-vyāpti*) when it has been practiced; what indeed is the purpose of a conceptualized knowledge of pervasion? (1.714)
Indeed, because it arises so rapidly, there is no discernment of it;
rather, it is merely inferred, and that itself is a conceptual construction. (1.715)
Alas! These whose intellects pride themselves on being logicians have begun to repeatedly forget even their own [position], blinded as they are by partiality for their own side. (1.716)
For according to your view, every cognition indeed perishes in a single moment;
it manifests its object merely by virtue of its own arising. (1.717)
Nothing other than a moment is said to possess the quality of being quickly produced; in reality, all that is consciousness which is indeed quickly produced. (1.718)
There would be no perception of any class of entities whatsoever, even for those with uninterrupted vision, over the course of an exceedingly long period of time. (1.719)

It is understood by him as well that, even at the mere moment of its arising, an object is manifested in such a way that its clarity as an objective field occurs solely by virtue of its production. (1.720)
How could its state of being both more rapid and stationary bring about differentiation, since that [consciousness], it is said, depends upon the senses, is self-luminous, and yet exists? (1.721)
In other cases, it functions as a means, like lightning or a lamp; likewise, in that very same [object], the state of being long-lasting or momentary appears for the sake of differentiation. (1.722)
Furthermore, in any inferences, there would be no apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, such that it could be observed as becoming manifest again and again. (1.723)
Furthermore, how could a series of cognitions of smoke and so forth, even if it clearly arises within the self, produce the manifestation of a single entity? (1.724)
Now, if the final knowledge of synthesis will act in this way, how can that too be distinct [from the object], being equal to the prior consciousness? (1.725)
If that [consciousness] were non-existent, it could not connect with the preceding series of cognitions; for no connection is possible once [the prior state] has perished. (1.726)
Now, if it is argued that here the "connecting" of cognitions must be nothing other than recollection, how indeed can that occur in the absence of experience? (1.727)
Furthermore, the experience of cognitions themselves is not possible anywhere, for it is your own view that two cognitions do not exist simultaneously. (1.728)

The nature of both cognition and the cognizable is observed as existing simultaneously; it is not the case for two things that arise in prior and posterior forms and are thus mutually contradictory. (1.729)

Therefore, even that cognition which is preceded by the appearance of the pervasion and its subsequent application, in that case as well, this perception is indeed a non-sequential experience of the object. (1.730)
Just as one who has suddenly awakened from deep sleep, with eyes opening wide, perceives things directly in order to remove the impurity of the objective aspect of existence. (1.731)
Just as one performing acts such as the cleansing of the eyes does not conceive of objects [as external], thinking "I infer them," so too should it be understood in this case as well. (1.732)
And just as one who has not awakened from the dense delusion of deep sleep forgets both his own self and that very place at that moment, so it is here. (1.733)
Then, having awakened his stainless self-vision through the accumulation of effort, he thinks, "I am that," according to the ultimate reality of consciousness. (1.734)
In all those cases, this Lord Bhairava, whose nature is consciousness, by virtue of his absolute freedom, conceals and reveals his own form.
To that extent, ignorance of this [object] ceases and cognition arises;
and since that [cognition] is vivid, let it be considered as being directly perceived by everyone. (1.736)
And when the word "jar" is heard, the cognition of its broad base, belly, and so forth likewise arises through the recollection of convention and other such factors. (1.737)
Just as in the examination of a gem, one's own consciousness, which is of a clear nature, remains while awakening it through the conjunctions with other cognitions. (1.738)
Then, through the union with the final, clearly awakened consciousness, the true nature of the jewel shines forth here; other cognitions have no utility in this regard. (1.739)
They extended their causality for the sake of awakening that very [consciousness];
for once it is engaged in the process of manifestation, they no longer have any utility.
From such an analogy as that of the ignorant jeweler, it is indeed clear that even in the case of verbal cognition, there is only a single manifesting consciousness. (1.741)
Therefore, when such a word is heard, that which immediately follows is this very cognition of such a nature regarding the manifestation of the object. (1.742)
That much of the object remains there, like the prior and posterior parts of a jar; for surely, that jar would be a single entity consisting of a composite whole. (1.743)
But there is no identity between word and object; how then can there be such a similarity?
Alas! Your eyes are clouded by the cataract of habitual grasping at difference. (1.744)
Even through the application of the collyrium of sound reasoning, one has not attained the stainless vision;
this Lord Bhairava is non-different from the state of being both the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

Since it has already been established previously that "the one whose form is ever complete [remains] by reflecting only upon the Self," how could there even be the possibility of this question? (1.746)
Thus, even in the case of analogy and other means of knowledge, it is clearly evident that in every instance it is consciousness itself, in the form of perception, that appears. 1.747.
Even a blind man, perceiving various forms through touch, sound, and so forth, clearly experiences that very same vividness in those respective instances. (1.748)

therefore, for those wishing to enter here, the Sage [prescribes it] by virtue of the sequence of formal requests (*jñapti*). (1.917)
The Blessed One himself has declared that the universe is none other than that [Self], since the freedom of undivided consciousness shines forth upon the path of duality. (1.918)
This established distinction between the one who is to be instructed and the instructor is extended [only as long as] one conceives that the Guru is one's own self and the deity is another. (1.919)
One considers one's own uttered words to be the words of another; likewise, one regards both the object to be communicated and that by which it is communicated as being external. (1.920)
For all that is indeed one's own nature, yet it is conceived as distinct, just like the state of the dream-path or the succession of instructions. (1.921)

Just as a dull-witted creature, upon hearing what is said by another, conceives of it as being true, so too is this entire worldly transaction [of the waking state] like one who is dreaming while still in the womb.
If it is asked, "What then would be the distinction between dreams and the waking state?", it will be stated again: "Or rather, what has not been taught by the independent Lord? (1.923).
Thus, by the very sequence of the formal motion (jñapti), there is a distinction between injunction and restatement;
for "the Lord is everything" and "everything is the Lord" are indeed one and the same. (1.924)
In reality, like a jar or a pot, the universe is merely a modification; "you alone are the denotable object of these"—thus did the illustrious Nārāyaṇa declare.
But if there is non-difference [between the two], how can there be the conceptual construction of injunction and restatement?
[The answer is: "That which has protruding teeth is this Caitra"—here, one first perceives the subject with protruding teeth. (1.926)
If the portion "Caitra" is restated and [the action] is what is enjoined, then that [action] would be distinct from Caitra, and Caitra would be distinct from that; how could this be? (1.927)
In such cases as "The pot is Caitra," there would be no distinction between affirmation and restatement;
therefore, the established position is that whatever is Caitra, he is the one with protruding teeth. (1.928)
The real injunction arising from mere cognition is employed for both prescriptions and restatements toward those who do not yet know the established usage of synonymous terms, as in:
"This is a tree (pādapa); it is a grower (bhūruha)."
Just as "pot" and "jar" are spoken of [as synonyms], so too Maheśvara is said to be "this entire world. (1.929)
Thus, through the yoga of the *saṃpuṭa*, there is indeed a state of complete fullness, within which hundreds of portions of both withdrawal and emanation remain contained. (1.930)
Some, desiring to worship that very [deity] in its parts through her, do so by means of four, six, twelve, and so forth, arising from the doubling of one and so on. (1.931)

Through various divisions consisting of the cycles of consciousness (*saṃviccakra*), that single consciousness is split by diverse sequences; it is one, yet it is twofold as the very nature of vision and action, and then it is threefold.
Furthermore, through the accompaniment of the power of manifestation (*pronmeṣa-śakti*), it is described as fourfold;
however, by virtue of its rootedness in the bliss of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), it is declared to be fivefold. (1.933)

However, through the investigation and deliberation upon the discourse of consciousness as spoken in the sixfold group of vowels, there is a twelvefold consciousness regarding the common objective domain at the beginning of creation and so forth. (1.934)
Because each one consists of a triad, or because the triad possesses a fourfold nature,
consciousness brings about creation and therein attains the state of redness (passion).
It brings about the destruction of persistence and may conceive doubt somewhere;
then, having withdrawn that portion of objective existence through its own power of withdrawal, it [re-creates] them again from itself.
Within that [state], the nature of being the destroyer is contemplated; through its own sovereignty, it does not desire either the rapid dissolution or the cessation of merit and demerit.

In this way, swallowing within herself the circle of rays that constitute the instruments for the portions of awakening, she withdraws the suns situated in the portions of the means of valid cognition.
Then, having withdrawn that portion consisting of the imagined into the unimagined heart— which, though transcending all that, resides within the undivided expanse— // 1.939 //
One should lead the universe out through the gateway of the eyes; having led it thus, one should then effect emanation, and so forth, by means of this sequential application. // 1.940 //
This wheel with twelve spokes revolves perpetually; for it, these [months] constitute its gross nature, being the perfection of the mass of months and so forth.
By virtue of the sequence and non-sequence, this wheel— arisen as twofold, threefold, manifold, and through various sequences and non-sequences— expands.
It devours the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, the cognition, and the knower. // 1.942 //
Due to the reliance upon the multitude of infinite rays contained within this wheel, the differentiation of these wheels can never be enumerated. (1.943)
For just as the white, yellow, red, and other colors on the wing of a peacock appear here, flashing and fading, though they do not possess that nature [of being real]. (1.944)
Thus, the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa), fully replete with subtle consciousness that has neither opened nor dissolved, shines forth, variegated by the mental fluctuations of closing and opening.

Is it then an incalculable number, or perhaps one in which each contains another within its womb?
Or is it not that wheel at all, but rather the single expanse of space itself unfolding?
That too shines forth either as containing within it infinite circles of existence, or as containing within it infinite space; it is called the single Great Space.
Just as the single sky shines forth in white, blue, and red,
and just as these clouds likewise appear in many ways,
so too does the reality of consciousness manifest through forms devoid of calculation or enumeration.
It manifests independently through its own forms, yet none of those [forms] exist as such. (1.949)
Thus did my Lord, dwelling within my heart, himself explain this reality, having realized it in its manifold forms.
It has been transmitted through the succession of the lineage of gurus. // 1.950 //
Therefore, since those who do not resort to the capacity for understanding in that system cannot grasp it,
surely the Lord exists for the sake of awakening them.
He has taught the various arrangements of the mandala. // 1.951 //

so too [is one introduced] by means of mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and tantras.

Even here, something shines forth by His will alone—
whether far away or nearby, possessing degrees of proximity,
yet untouched by them and established in a partless state.
Thus, there are indeed many different varieties within the chapter on ritual action.

Because even a mere fraction of it exists in manifold ways within the supreme state, the Supreme, whose form is that of the Lord of Mantras, is intensified by the nature of being both transcendent and immanent.

since it is not a real thing but merely a distinction of limiting conditions (upādhi), how could it be so conceptualized? (1.994)
For he who is superior in qualities to all others is therefore the Supreme Lord;
thus spoke the one who has fashioned the entire sphere of space and time from his own bliss.

This Śāmbhava means is non-instrumental (anupāya), for it is the means consisting of consciousness (cid-upāya). Beyond that, the Āṇava means is insentient (jaḍa-upāya), and it is considered to be of many kinds.

therefore, the channels, the sense organs, and external objects serve as means for consciousness.
In that regard, whatever apprehension of external forms occurs by relying on the activity of the senses—that is clearly waking consciousness, which persists again and again. (1.999)
Dream is a creation fashioned by one's own mental constructs; it is the inversion of the waking state.
It is the experience of the *layākala* [state], which occurs due to the force of residual karma from dissolution, and not otherwise. (1.100)

Due to the absence of night, he would remain steadfast; for one who is asleep and does not experience pleasure or pain, [this occurs] due to the impurity of the *jñānākala*, arising solely from the experience [of karma]. (1.1001)
Those possessing differentiation—both insentient and sentient—are intended to be differentiated by themselves;
therein, within the Fourth state, reside the three: the Mantras, their Lords (Tannāthas), and the Supreme Lords (Adhīśvaras).
Until they are capable of entering the portion of the awakening of Bhairava,
phenomena— whose own essence has dissolved— are themselves non-dual.
"In the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which consists of fifteen aspects, whatever form appears clearly to whom, let that be considered waking. (1.1004)

That fourth state, which arises by virtue of the synthesis of the triad and is like the thread of a garland, should be recognized as present in all distinctions. (1.1006)

"That which shines with the fullness of non-duality, in which all distinctions have been dissolved—that they call 'beyond the fourth' (turyātīta); one should apply this [definition] everywhere. 1.1007

For at the time of dissolution, one's own true nature is the waking state, while the states prior to that, such as dreaming and so forth, follow in succession; thus the wise person should trace this entire sequence everywhere.
Even when the Lord is fully present in one place, that which transcends the fourth state is called bliss; the fourth state is desire itself, while deep sleep is the ground of the seed.
Knowledge is the state of dreaming, while action is remembered as the waking state;
herein lie the designations arising from the stages of yoga, such as "abiding in the body" (piṇḍasthatā) and so forth.
However, the Sarvatobhadra and other [mandalas] are constructed by those possessing the knowledge of *prasaṃkhyāna*, because each one consists of four forms; therefore, they are extensive. (1.1011)
The fourfold form is unified in one; thereafter, there is a triad and then oneness.
Yet the Lord Bhairava alone is the one whose nature is the radiantly manifest universe.
This entire path, beginning with Śiva and ending with the totality (sakala), is unified within Bhairava, existing in a state of non-differentiation from Him.
Attaining autonomy through that [divine] autonomy, He manifests;
this very state, residing within the nature of the subject, is conceived as the path of mantra (mantrādhvan). // 1.1014 //
By virtue of its nature as valid cognition (*pramā*), this is defined as the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*);
having attained the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it proceeds to become the path of words (*padādhvan*). (1.1015)

Without abandoning its immersion in the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), yet proceeding toward the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatā*) through the application of conceptualization, the path of the *kalās* is conjoined with the subject (*mātṛ*). (1.1016)

When it is pure and conjoined with the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*), let it be understood as the path of reality (*tattvādhvan*); when it is conjoined with the state of being the substratum for grossness, it is described as the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*). (1.1017)

For when the state of the signified is swallowed by the reflective awareness of consciousness (cid-vimarśa), it becomes intent upon the protection of the mind, which is dependent on the knowledge and action of Śiva.
Through the skillful intensity of his passion for the playful display of the entire multitude of powers,
the path of mantra, whose essence is Śiva, suddenly and swiftly emerged first.
Through resting in the pure experience of surging consciousness, yogis possess unimpeded powers due to their capacity for all designations. (1.1020)
Having been created, their functions extend from their own selves up to the objects and the earth;
thus, within their own self, they perceive that many objects in the play of consciousness within their own being.

Even children and animal subjects who do not participate in linguistic convention possess a true consciousness that reflects the nature of valid cognition when they perceive through direct touch. (1.1022)

Relying upon this self-awareness, which consists of the essence of non-artificial mental formations (*saṃskāra*) yet appears as variously differentiated, they too attain a manifold state of subjectivity. (1.1023)
If even those linguistic conventions attain firm establishment within this uncontrived consciousness of infinite colors, they too come to function as non-conventional.
But without this [consciousness], all the numerous conventions established would never find rest in the mind, due to their connection with other conventions. (1.1025)
Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress because it would result in the destruction of the very root;
for even in that case, how indeed could a child be taught the conventional designation?
Therefore, that infinite and non-illusory collection of phonemes, which is of such a nature, always unfolds in full expansion, accompanied by the reflective awareness of consciousness.

For instance, when the words of another are heard, the dull-witted person whose own cognition is obstructed does not attain the status of a knower regarding that object. (1.1029)

Then, until there is eternal rest for the Lord, he simultaneously brings forth many phonemes that are well-established as fulfilling the portions of experience.

Thus, it is certain that the state of being an object of knowledge, the status of the knower, and the nature of the means of knowledge likewise belong to this collection of thirty-six principles that constitute the Self. (1.1036)
In that regard, all this shines within the eternal Supreme Lord in the form of a reflection, and not as something external, because [He is its source]. (1.1037)
Within the auspicious sky of consciousness alone, such notions as various bodies and so forth appear as distinct to transmigrating beings, just as a snake and the like appear in a rope. (1.1038)

Whether the discipline has been firmly rooted through its total eradication [of obstacles] and its continuous practice, or even if it is not yet firmly rooted, this Bhairava of the sky of consciousness remains independent. (1.1043)

Just as no other agent is established by any means of valid cognition in a dream, so too should the creation be understood as arising from one's own independent self-awareness. 1.1045
Indeed, he who plays thus in the variegated garden-city of the mind understands: "I alone exist as these entities, which are composed of pure consciousness. (1.1046)
Thus, "I am born" and "I am dead"—these various manifestations of birth and death appear upon the wall of the mind, imagined by oneself, even though there is neither birth nor death. (1.1047)
The distinction between this world and the next is merely a cognition of "otherness"; however, the cognition of timelessness remains undivided even amidst the differences of space.

In the discussion regarding the relationship between the container and the contained among the categories beginning with the gross elements and the subtle elements,

From this very habitual identification such as "I am dense," the state of being earth and so forth arises;

Therefore, he who is the Lord because of his sovereignty—capable of thus emptying existent entities and manifesting non-existent ones—is the Supreme Lord. 1.1059

And since this has already been stated previously, it will not be analyzed further; moreover, the refutation of external objects has been extensively elaborated by many [authorities]. (1.1061)

But those scholars who dispute here, their roots of ignorance being unperceived, are surely intent on protecting their own mental constructs. (1.1065)

"May my own afflictions be better than causing suffering to another"—this is the fruit conceived by him as the result of such arduous asceticism. (1.1079)
"Garlic and such things are declared inedible; let living beings indeed accept that such a command is simply without reason. (1.1080)

Thus, in this way, a difference in opinion regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten—such as swans, fish, and so forth—is appropriate; otherwise, it would not be possible in any way whatsoever. (1.1081)
Thus, whether in the seen or the unseen, through the sequence of imagined parts and sub-parts,
that very same connection with the fruit is established today, rooted in the ground of consciousness.
"The body exists in the world beyond the physical mass; it is not otherwise"—such is the established doctrine.
Is it that living beings are "bearers of bodies" because they are not mutually connected? // 1.1083 //
By means of all those multitudes of treatises, the stake of doubt was driven into the ground;
mounted upon the soil of the ignorant mind, it has reached the point of fruition.
"I have a donor today; through the sequence of giving alms-food, I have thus attained the expansion of my limbs, and with a full body, I am well-established. (1.1085)

"By means of an unseen action (adṛṣṭa-kriyā) fashioned through [the roles of] son, disciple, or one's own self, I am destined for heaven and remain perfectly established in the enjoyment of my acquisitions. (1.1086)
I have no one to provide me with alms, and I myself am a great evildoer;
there is no protector for me anywhere—I am falling into the ocean of hell.
"Sometime, somehow, there will be a savior for me"—such an expansion of cognitions bears fruit by itself in that very way. (1.1088)
But let there be no one for her to offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and so forth; nevertheless, she experiences that fruit which is fashioned by her own volition, just as it manifests.
But this mind, firmly bound within by the cement of the thunderbolt of doubt,
is consumed with its very roots in an instant by the fire of Bhairava alone.
"I am indeed Śiva, the blazing fire that consumes the dream-house of saṃsāra, which contains within its womb all manner of diverse consciousnesses without exception. // 1.1091 //
Thus, that deluded one, whose consciousness has become diversified by the perception of karma, falsely imagines the very process of volition to be the manifold cycle of existence.
Therefore, a child who dies devoid of other latent impressions (vāsanā) would become a mere infant again, whereas one whose firm worldly impressions (saṃsāra-vāsanā) are dormant [would not]. (1.1093)
Those [elements] likewise persist until youth is reached again through the sequence of those very latent impressions (vāsanā). // 1.1094 //

Through the latent impressions of formative volitions (saṃskāra), someone— though rendered insentient by the impressions of dullness— is conceitedly attached to various transmigrations, as if by the winds of space.
Through its conjunction with earth and water, it attains the nature of flowers and fruits;
once consumed, it returns to the state of an embryo in the form of vital seed (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, as long as one repeatedly conceives of the various states of saṃsāra, Śiva alone remains permeated by the latent impressions of his own formative forces (saṃskāra). 1.1097.
He experiences enjoyments fashioned by his own autonomy in various heavens and hells; sometimes these consist of earth, sometimes of water, and sometimes are a mixture of both.
Thus, this consciousness, consisting of the world, shines by its own nature;
wherever it is sustained, there itself pleasure and so forth arise from its own latent impressions.
He knows [them], yet he cannot be seen by another; but he knows others in a different way.
In the ultimate sense, there is neither space nor any time whatsoever.

For in the theory of difference (bhedavāda), the state of being the whole or a part [of space] arises from the location of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) itself; thus, even the location of the adjunct is distinct. (1.1101)
Thus, since they depend upon one another, there is no spatial distinction whatsoever;
therefore, it is perfectly consistent that the difference in their own essential natures (svarūpa) alone constitutes the differentiator.

And that [non-existence] does not apply to those things whose sole nature is luminosity; this has been established by this very same perspective of reflective awareness (parāmarśa), which excludes them. (1.1103)
They were made to feel apprehensive by a flood of suspicious scriptures;
thus absorbed in them, they were tormented by the conceptualizations of infinite inert beings created within their own dreams.
Those devoid of awakening are made to grasp groundless doubts through fallacious treatises, just as consciousness, though long remaining latent, awakens once again. (1.1105)

Nevertheless, it bears fruit; thus, by means of such [means] as prescribed expiations and so forth, [the Lord acts] through His sovereignty consisting in the freedom to manifest multiplicity. (1.1106)

Whatever has been fashioned as that very [object] assumes the form of a body and so forth, through the occurrence of erroneous appearances corrupted by the appearance of cold and other such sensations. (1.1107)
Then, when the channels and so forth are afflicted by contraction, expansion, striking, and the like, the great machine of the bellows-body— the wheel of vital winds— becomes otherwise.

By that [means], the vital breath (prāṇa) ceases within the inert-seeming body, either when authority over it has passed away or previously, through the sequence of latent impressions (vāsanā). // 1.1109 //
In that very state, one may imagine an enjoyment designated as the "other world," or one perceives it as being like a stone; yet again, one awakens.

And because it is conventionally established that "this world is other," its status as belonging to another world consists of heaven, liberation, and so forth, exactly as they are conventionally established in the mind here.
In exactly the same way, it appears externally; therefore, even there, there is diversity:
bondage, liberation, happiness, heaven, suffering, and the state consisting of insentience.
In this way, consciousness alone, being independent, shines forth as the nature of Śiva;
just as the state of "I" persists to the same extent even when [the self] is further endowed with constituent parts.
Likewise, my state of being resides within the form of Bhairava, which consists of the universe;
even as a child, one perceives a Vetāla in the void as one who accomplishes real purposes.
Thus, the variety of objects such as those to be meditated upon or worshipped performs purposeful action;
yet the embodied [individual], though distinct, having been summoned, instantly abandons his own enjoyments. (1.1115)
"O King, 'it comes'—this report is fitting only for words;
however, all this [notion] of its being formless and so forth is logically consistent. (1.1116)
For the Self itself, having become such, shines forth as such through differentiation; this very nature belongs to consciousness, and it is that alone. (1.1117)
In the scripture, karmic impurity (kārma-mala) is defined by its being permeated by differentiation;
however, when engaged in rituals such as initiation (dīkṣā), it does not extend the status of being an impurity.
For he has undertaken the vow of burning away the entire transmigratory existence consisting of duality;
and initiation, in reality, consists of such a nature of true consciousness.
Thus it has been stated in the Unsurpassed Method (*anuttara-naya*): "He who knows thus according to reality;
for when the sphere of duality has been stilled through the yoga of such realization... (1.1120).
The Self alone is Śiva, the One; what bondage is there, and what liberation?
Nevertheless, this is taught for the purpose of entering the great consciousness of initiation.

That initiation, which has action as its intrinsic nature, is for the sake of removing the impurities of karma and so forth, regarding those actions projected by the force of necessity established by one's own nature. (1.1122)
Since his enjoyment is performed simultaneously through the power of mantra, so too are the determinations of space, time, and the paths of the breath within him. (1.1123)
His lineages extend from the earth up to Śiva;
therein alone they partake in birth, enjoyment, authority, and dissolution. (1.1124)
Having been established [in one state], he is drawn out from there and enjoined elsewhere;
thus, through mutual [action] between the teacher, whose self-nature is rooted in certain consciousness, and the disciple.
Initiation, which consists of a mind free from ritual action, indeed arrests all the powers of prior karma.
Even there, the continuous sequence of rice, sesame, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, and so forth— though fashioned by the weight of the Śaiva doctrine of necessity—
is not a mere nocturnal fabrication, for its words are perfectly clear.
Even though it has reached a state of being rootless, because its functioning is characterized by differentiation. // 1.1126 //

Even though there is a distinction, this [state] is nevertheless pure because it is the cause for the destruction of future merit and so forth that produce further saṃsāra; therefore, for that very reason, it is the net of reality.
Everything exists in two ways alone, by virtue of abiding as either pure or otherwise. // 1.1127 //

Indeed, the pure [Self], inlaid with the three powers, shines forth as the couple (yāmala); thus, by virtue of the conceptualization of the activity of action, this manifold expansion of necessity (niyatiprapañca) is produced in many ways.
The connection with such enjoyment is produced by something other than that which is extremely subtle. // 1.1128 //
The assembly of mudrās and maṇḍalas, adorned with mantras and tantras, wherein all practices such as yoga become capable of bestowing the fruit. // 1.1129 //
Firmly established in their desire for the attainment of the fruit of liberation, they regard here nothing other than uninterruptedness itself as the fruit. (1.1130)
For when there is no cutting off of the infinite and the endless, there is no conception of sacrifice and so forth, nor any unbounded desire.
Nevertheless, those whose vision has transcended all [dualistic] views [perceive] that reality which is known to be supremely beautiful in its non-duality.

Due to the sovereign freedom of the nature of consciousness, some possess a desire for fruits; with reference to those very [desires], everything from the earth element upwards is provided for their fulfillment. (1.1133)
The *Dhāraṇāgrantha* is said here to extend up to Śiva through many divisions;
for indeed, there is nothing here that does not manifest as reality, as is the case in other systems.
Therefore, for those who abide here in the state of truth, what possibility is there of falling into a state that is to be abandoned? // 1.1134 //
Thus, that reality which manifests as the final topic of the seventeen chapters has been determined; for those desiring to attain the unsurpassed state of Śiva,
all of this has been proclaimed here in the *Jagadānanda* as being of the nature of the opposing side.
For it is because this entire phenomenal world exists here with differentiation as its very life-breath. // 1.1135 //
